f: 547. What happens to agency when a partner dies?
b: Agency is terminated.

f: 548. Why does termination of agency end the partnership?
b: Because the partnership cannot continue without the agency relationship that supports it.

f: 549. What happens to a partnership when one of its essential elements, agency, ends?
b: The partnership is dissolved.

f: 550. When is a partnership terminated due to apostasy?
b: It is terminated when an apostate joins the Abode of War and the judge formally rules that he has entered it.

f: 551. Why is joining the Abode of War treated like death regarding partnership?
b: Because legally it is treated as death, as previously explained.

f: 552. Does it matter whether the remaining partner knows of his partner’s death for the partnership to end?
b: No. The partnership ends regardless of whether he knows or not.

f: 553. Why does the partnership end without the remaining partner’s knowledge?
b: Because the termination occurs automatically by operation of law (ʿazl ḥukmī).

f: 554. What happens when agency in a partnership is terminated?
b: The partnership is also dissolved.

f: 555. What is ʿazl ḥukmī?
b: It is the termination of agency imposed automatically by law rather than by a person’s deliberate action.

f: 556. How does automatic termination of agency differ from voluntary dissolution of partnership?
b: Automatic termination occurs by law, while voluntary dissolution occurs through intentional revocation.

f: 557. If one partner voluntarily dissolves a partnership containing dirhams and dinars, when does the dissolution take effect?
b: It takes effect when the other partner becomes aware of it.

f: 558. Why does voluntary dissolution require the other partner’s knowledge?
b: Because it is an intentional revocation (ʿazl qaṣdī), not an automatic legal termination.

f: 559. What is ʿazl qaṣdī?
b: It is the deliberate revocation of agency or partnership by a person’s choice.

f: 560. Why is knowledge required in ʿazl qaṣdī but not in ʿazl ḥukmī?
b: Because deliberate revocation depends on communication, while automatic legal termination occurs immediately by law.

f: 561. May one partner pay the Zakāh due on the other partner’s wealth without permission?
b: No.

f: 562. Why may a partner not pay another partner’s Zakāh without permission?
b: Because paying Zakāh is not among the normal activities of commerce.

f: 563. Is payment of Zakāh included in the authority of partnership agency?
b: No. It requires separate authorization.

f: 564. If partners authorize each other to pay Zakāh, and both pay it one after another, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The second payer must reimburse the amount paid.

f: 565. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, does the second payer’s liability depend on knowing that the first payer already paid?
b: No. He is liable whether he knew or did not know.

f: 566. What situation is being discussed regarding two Zakāh payments?
b: A situation where the payments occur one after another.

f: 567. If both authorized partners pay Zakāh simultaneously, what happens according to the discussion?
b: Each must reimburse the other for the amount he paid on his behalf.

f: 568. Does the same disagreement apply to a Zakāh distributor appointed by another person?
b: Yes.

f: 569. If a person appointed to distribute Zakāh gives it to the poor after the owner already paid it, is the same disagreement applied?
b: Yes.

f: 570. What did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad say regarding the second Zakāh payer who did not know of the first payment?
b: He is not liable for reimbursement.

f: 571. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad say the unaware second payer is not liable?
b: Because the agent fulfilled his instruction by transferring ownership of the Zakāh to a poor recipient.

f: 572. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what determines whether the payment counts as Zakāh?
b: The principal’s intention, not the agent’s intention.

f: 573. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what is the agent responsible for?
b: Only what is within his ability to perform.

f: 574. What analogy did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad use for the Zakāh agent who unknowingly pays after the obligation was already fulfilled?
b: The case of an agent slaughtering the sacrifice for a person prevented from completing pilgrimage (dam al-iḥṣār).

f: 575. In the dam al-iḥṣār analogy, when is the agent not liable?
b: When the principal later completes the pilgrimage after the impediment ends, and the agent had already slaughtered without knowing.

f: 576. Why is the agent not liable in the dam al-iḥṣār analogy?
b: Because he performed the task assigned to him within his ability.

f: 577. What was Abū Ḥanīfah’s رحمه الله response regarding the Zakāh agent?
b: He argued that the agent was specifically instructed to discharge the obligation of Zakāh.

f: 578. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, why is the second Zakāh payer liable?
b: Because his specific duty was to discharge the Zakāh obligation, not merely transfer ownership of property.

f: 579. What is the key disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله/Muḥammad regarding the Zakāh agent?
b: Whether the agent’s duty is only transferring ownership or actually fulfilling the Zakāh obligation.

f: 580. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, why is the second Zakāh payment by an agent invalid as Zakāh?
b: Because the payment no longer fulfills the Zakāh obligation after the owner has already paid it.

f: 581. Why did the Zakāh agent fail to fulfill his instruction according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because his instruction was to discharge the owner’s Zakāh obligation, not merely to transfer ownership of money to a poor person.

f: 582. What was the purpose of authorizing another person to pay Zakāh?
b: The purpose was to relieve the owner of his legal obligation.

f: 583. Why does a person normally spend wealth in a voluntary act like paying through an agent?
b: Because he seeks to remove an existing obligation.

f: 584. Once the owner himself paid the Zakāh, what happened to the purpose of the agent’s authorization?
b: The purpose had already been achieved.

f: 585. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, when does the Zakāh agent’s authority end?
b: It ends automatically once the obligation has already been fulfilled.

f: 586. Why does the Zakāh agent’s authority end even if he does not know the Zakāh was already paid?
b: Because it is revoked by operation of law (ʿazl ḥukmī).

f: 587. What is the difference between ʿazl ḥukmī and ordinary revocation?
b: ʿAzl ḥukmī occurs automatically by law, without requiring knowledge of the agent.

f: 588. Do scholars agree that the same ruling applies to the sacrifice of one prevented from completing pilgrimage (dam al-iḥṣār)?
b: No. Some applied the same disagreement, while others distinguished between the two cases.

f: 589. What distinction do some scholars make between Zakāh and dam al-iḥṣār?
b: Zakāh must be discharged immediately, whereas the pilgrim may wait until the impediment is removed.

f: 590. Why is the authorization in the Zakāh case centered on discharge of the obligation?
b: Because Zakāh payment is immediately required.

f: 591. Why is the authorization in the dam al-iḥṣār case different?
b: Because the sacrifice is not immediately required if the pilgrim can wait until the obstacle ends.

f: 592. What happens if a partner in mufāwaḍah authorizes his partner to purchase a slave-girl for intercourse and the purchase is made?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, the slave-girl belongs exclusively to the purchasing partner without reimbursement.

f: 593. What did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad say regarding the purchase of a slave-girl for intercourse in mufāwaḍah?
b: They said the purchasing partner must reimburse his partner for half of the purchase price.

f: 594. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad require reimbursement in the slave-girl case?
b: Because the partner used jointly owned funds to pay a debt that belonged only to himself.

f: 595. What analogy did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad use for the slave-girl purchase?
b: They compared it to purchasing food and clothing for personal use.

f: 596. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, who owns the slave-girl after purchase?
b: The partner who was authorized to have intercourse with her owns her exclusively.

f: 597. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad say ownership belongs exclusively to the purchasing partner?
b: Because the purchase price corresponds to ownership of the slave-girl.

f: 598. What is Abū Ḥanīfah’s رحمه الله response to the argument of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: He argues that partnership rules initially make the slave-girl jointly owned.

f: 599. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, can partners alter the normal legal consequence of the partnership contract?
b: No. They cannot change the legal effect established by the partnership contract.

f: 600. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the default ruling when a slave-girl is purchased with partnership funds?
b: She initially enters the partnership as jointly owned property.

f: 601. Why does permission for intercourse imply transfer of the other partner’s share according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because intercourse is only lawful through ownership.

f: 602. How is the transfer of the partner’s share understood according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: It is understood as an implied gift contained within the permission.

f: 603. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله reject treating the transaction as a purchase of the partner’s share?
b: Because that would contradict the normal legal consequences of the partnership contract.

f: 604. How does the slave-girl case differ from food and clothing purchased by a partner?
b: Food and clothing are excluded from partnership rules by necessity, while the slave-girl initially enters joint ownership.

f: 605. Why does a partner who purchases food and clothing with partnership funds owe reimbursement?
b: Because those items belong exclusively to him from the beginning, so he paid his own debt with partnership property.

f: 606. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله not require reimbursement in the slave-girl case?
b: Because the purchase discharged a debt binding upon both partners initially, not only one partner.

f: 607. In either the slave-girl case or food and clothing case, whom may the seller demand payment from?
b: The seller may demand payment from either partner.

f: 608. Is there disagreement among the scholars about the seller’s right to recover the price from either partner in this case?
b: No. There is unanimous agreement.

f: 609. Why may the seller recover from either partner in mufāwaḍah?
b: Because the debt arose from a commercial transaction and mufāwaḍah includes mutual guarantee.

f: 610. What principle of mufāwaḍah makes both partners liable for commercial debts?
b: Mutual guarantee (kafālah).

f: 611. Why is the slave-girl purchase treated like food and clothing regarding seller liability?
b: Because both arise from commercial purchases covered by the guarantee of mufāwaḍah.

f: 1. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, when does the ownership of the endower cease after establishing a waqf?
b: It does not cease merely by declaring the waqf unless a judge confirms it or it is made contingent upon the endower’s death.

f: 2. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what two situations make a waqf binding?
b: A judicial ruling confirming it, or making it effective upon the endower’s death.

f: 3. Give an example of a waqf contingent upon death.
b: Saying, "When I die, my house shall be a waqf for such-and-such."

f: 4. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, when does the endower's ownership cease?
b: Immediately upon declaring the waqf.

f: 5. According to Muḥammad, when does the endower's ownership cease?
b: After appointing a trustee and delivering the waqf property into the trustee's possession.

f: 6. What does the word waqf mean linguistically?
b: It means to withhold or restrain.

f: 7. What expressions are given as examples of the linguistic meaning of waqf?
b: "I stopped the animal (waqaftu al-dābbah)" and "I caused the animal to stop (awqaftuhā)."

f: 8. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the legal definition of waqf?
b: Restraining the corpus of the property while ownership remains with the endower and donating its usufruct.

f: 9. To what contract does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله compare waqf?
b: A loan for use (ʿāriyah).

f: 10. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, who owns the waqf property after the declaration?
b: The endower continues to own it.

f: 11. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is donated in a waqf?
b: The usufruct (benefit) of the property.

f: 12. Why did some scholars claim that waqf is invalid according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because usufruct is not a tangible object, so they argued that donating it is invalid.

f: 13. What wording in al-Aṣl led some scholars to think Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله considered waqf invalid?
b: Al-Aṣl contains wording suggesting waqf is entirely invalid.

f: 14. What is the sounder interpretation of Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله opinion regarding waqf?
b: Waqf is valid but not binding.

f: 15. According to the sounder opinion, what contract does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله liken waqf to?
b: A loan for use (ʿāriyah), which is valid but not binding.

f: 16. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, how is waqf legally defined?
b: Restraining the corpus of the property under the ownership of Allah Most High.

f: 17. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what happens to the endower's ownership?
b: It ceases and the property is dedicated to Allah while its benefits remain for His servants.

f: 18. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, does waqf become binding?
b: Yes. It becomes permanently binding.

f: 19. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, may waqf property be sold?
b: No.

f: 20. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, may waqf property be gifted?
b: No.

f: 21. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, may waqf property be inherited?
b: No.

f: 22. Why can the word waqf support both the Hanafī definitions?
b: Because its wording linguistically accommodates both meanings.

f: 23. How should preference between the different definitions of waqf be determined?
b: By examining the legal evidence.

f: 24. What ḥadīth did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad use as evidence for their view of waqf?
b: The Prophet ﷺ told ʿUmar رضي الله عنه regarding his land: "Retain the corpus of the property. It is not to be sold, inherited, or given away."

f: 25. To whom was the Prophet ﷺ speaking in the ḥadīth about waqf?
b: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رضي الله عنه (رضي الله عنه).

f: 26. Which land did ʿUmar رضي الله عنه wish to dedicate as waqf?
b: His land known as Thamgh.

f: 27. According to the ḥadīth, what must happen to the corpus of waqf property?
b: It must be retained and not disposed of.

f: 28. According to the ḥadīth, what three transactions are prohibited regarding waqf property?
b: It may not be sold, inherited, or given away.

f: 29. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad argue that waqf should become permanently binding?
b: So that the donor's reward continues without interruption.

f: 30. How is perpetual reward achieved according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: By removing the donor's ownership and dedicating the property to Allah.

f: 31. What analogy do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad use to support the permanence of waqf?
b: The legal status of a mosque.

f: 32. Why is a mosque used as an analogy for waqf?
b: Because it is permanently dedicated to Allah and removed from private ownership.

f: 33. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, why should waqf be treated like a mosque?
b: Because both involve dedicating property to Allah for the continuing benefit of His servants.

f: 34. What ḥadīth did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله cite as evidence regarding waqf?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no withholding of property that prevents the prescribed shares established by Allah."

f: 35. What statement of Shurayḥ did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله use as evidence regarding waqf?
b: "Muḥammad ﷺ came with the sale of property that had been declared inalienable."

f: 36. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, who continues to own the property after establishing a waqf?
b: The endower (wāqif).

f: 37. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what demonstrates that ownership remains with the endower?
b: He may continue benefiting from the property through cultivation, residence, and other lawful uses.

f: 38. What kinds of personal benefit may the endower continue to enjoy according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Cultivation, residence, and other lawful forms of use.

f: 39. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, how does the endower's authority to administer the waqf indicate continued ownership?
b: His authority to direct its revenues and appoint supervisors shows that ownership remains with him.

f: 40. What administrative powers does the endower retain over a waqf according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: He may direct its revenues to their intended purposes and appoint supervisors over it.

f: 41. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what exactly is donated in a waqf?
b: The usufruct (benefit) of the property.

f: 42. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله compare waqf to a loan for use (ʿāriyah)?
b: Because ownership remains with the owner while only the usufruct is donated.

f: 43. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, why must ownership remain with the endower for continuing charity to exist?
b: Because the continuing donation of the property's income depends upon his ownership.

f: 44. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله argue that ownership cannot simply be removed from the endower?
b: Because the Sharīʿah does not legislate transferring ownership while the property itself remains intact.

f: 45. To which pre-Islamic institution does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله compare this issue?
b: The institution of the sā'ibah.

f: 46. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish waqf from emancipation?
b: Because emancipation destroys ownership by ending the proprietary relationship itself, whereas waqf does not.

f: 47. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish waqf from a mosque?
b: Because a mosque is dedicated exclusively to Allah, while a waqf still retains human rights over the property.

f: 48. Why may no one derive personal benefit from a mosque?
b: Because it is devoted exclusively to Allah.

f: 49. Why does a waqf not become exclusively devoted to Allah according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because human rights over the property have not been completely severed.

f: 50. According to the text, when does the endower's ownership cease?
b: Only if a judge confirms the waqf or if it is made contingent upon death.

f: 51. Why is a judge's ruling effective in making a waqf binding?
b: Because it resolves a matter over which the jurists legitimately disagreed.

f: 52. According to the sounder opinion, does making a waqf contingent upon death remove the endower's ownership?
b: No. His ownership still does not cease.

f: 53. According to the sounder opinion, what happens when a waqf is made contingent upon death?
b: The endower permanently donates the usufruct of the property.

f: 54. To what is a waqf contingent upon death compared according to the sounder opinion?
b: A perpetual bequest of usufruct.

f: 55. Why does a waqf contingent upon death become binding according to the sounder opinion?
b: Because it resembles a perpetual bequest of usufruct.

f: 56. What type of judge is intended by the text when discussing confirmation of a waqf?
b: A duly appointed judicial authority.

f: 57. Did the jurists agree that an arbitrator's (muḥakkam's) ruling has the same effect as a judge's ruling?
b: No. They differed on this issue.

f: 58. How did al-Ṭaḥāwī classify a waqf established during terminal illness?
b: He treated it like a bequest that takes effect after death.

f: 59. According to the sounder opinion, what is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله ruling on a waqf established during terminal illness?
b: It is not binding.

f: 60. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, is a waqf established during terminal illness binding?
b: Yes, but only up to one-third of the estate.

f: 61. To what extent is a terminal-illness waqf effective according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: Only to one-third of the estate.

f: 62. How much of a healthy person's property can a waqf affect?
b: It takes effect from the entirety of his property.

f: 63. What is the difference between a waqf established during health and one established during terminal illness?
b: A healthy person's waqf may affect all of his property, whereas a terminal-illness waqf is limited to one-third according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad.

f: 64. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what is the basic ruling regarding ownership after a valid waqf?
b: The endower's ownership is removed.

f: 65. What is the disagreement between Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding ownership in a waqf?
b: They differ on how and when ownership is removed.

f: 66. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, when does ownership cease in a waqf?
b: Immediately upon the declaration of the waqf.

f: 67. Which other jurist agrees with Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله that ownership ceases immediately upon declaration of a waqf?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī.

f: 68. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله compare waqf to emancipation?
b: Because both involve relinquishing ownership.

f: 69. According to Muḥammad, what additional step is required before ownership ceases in a waqf?
b: The property must be delivered to the appointed trustee or administrator.

f: 70. Why does Muḥammad require delivery of the waqf property to a trustee?
b: Because waqf is a right belonging to Allah, and such rights are realized through delivery to a human recipient.

f: 71. Why can't property be transferred directly to Allah as an independent legal act?
b: Because direct legal transfer to Allah is not possible; it is realized indirectly through a trustee.

f: 72. According to Muḥammad, to what does waqf resemble because of the requirement of delivery?
b: Zakāh and voluntary charity.

f: 73. Once a waqf is valid according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, who owns the property?
b: It leaves the ownership of the endower but does not enter the ownership of the beneficiary.

f: 74. Why does a waqf not become the beneficiary's property?
b: Because otherwise the beneficiary could freely sell it.

f: 75. What legal consequence would follow if the beneficiary became the owner of the waqf property?
b: He would have unrestricted authority to sell it.

f: 76. Why can't a former owner permanently restrict the powers of a new owner?
b: Because ownership cannot be restricted by conditions imposed by a former owner after ownership has transferred.

f: 77. What does the inability of the beneficiary to sell the waqf prove?
b: That the property never enters the beneficiary's ownership.

f: 78. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what remains with the endower after establishing a waqf?
b: Ownership of the corpus remains with the endower, while the usufruct is permanently dedicated.

f: 79. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is permanently dedicated in a waqf?
b: The usufruct of the property.

f: 80. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, is the waqf of an undivided share in jointly owned property valid?
b: Yes.

f: 81. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله permit a waqf of undivided jointly owned property?
b: Because partition merely completes possession, and possession is not a condition for a valid waqf according to him.

f: 82. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, is taking possession (qabḍ) a condition for the validity of waqf?
b: No.

f: 83. According to Muḥammad, is a waqf of an undivided share in divisible property valid?
b: No.

f: 84. Why does Muḥammad invalidate a waqf of an undivided share in divisible property?
b: Because taking possession is a condition, and partition is necessary to complete possession.

f: 85. To what type of property does the disagreement over an undivided waqf primarily relate?
b: Property capable of physical partition.

f: 86. According to Muḥammad, is a waqf of an undivided share in indivisible property valid?
b: Yes.

f: 87. Why does Muḥammad permit a waqf of an undivided share in indivisible property?
b: Because such property is treated like completed gifts (hibah) and completed charitable donations (ṣadaqah).

f: 88. What two kinds of waqf are exceptions even according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: A mosque and a graveyard.

f: 89. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, is a waqf of an undivided share in a mosque valid?
b: No.

f: 90. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, is a waqf of an undivided share in a graveyard valid?
b: No.

f: 91. Does the invalidity of an undivided waqf in a mosque or graveyard apply even when the property cannot be physically divided?
b: Yes.

f: 92. Why is an undivided waqf of a mosque or graveyard invalid?
b: Because continued joint ownership prevents the property from becoming exclusively devoted to Allah.

f: 93. What legal principle prevents an undivided mosque or graveyard from becoming a valid waqf?
b: Exclusive dedication to Allah cannot coexist with continuing joint ownership.

f: 94. Why is alternating use (muhāyā'ah) unacceptable for a mosque or graveyard held in joint ownership?
b: Because it would lead to highly objectionable alternating uses incompatible with their sacred purpose.

f: 95. What example illustrates the problem of alternating use in a jointly owned graveyard?
b: Using it as a graveyard one year and cultivating it the next.

f: 96. What example illustrates the problem of alternating use in a jointly owned mosque?
b: Using it as a mosque at one time and as a stable at another.

f: 97. Why does the problem of alternating use not apply to an ordinary charitable endowment?
b: Because its income can be generated and divided between the owners.

f: 98. According to Muḥammad, what happens if the owner endows an entire property and part of it is later successfully claimed by another person?
b: The waqf becomes invalid with respect to the remainder.

f: 99. Why does Muḥammad invalidate the remaining waqf when part of the endowed property is successfully claimed?
b: Because the resulting joint ownership is treated as though it existed from the outset.

f: 100. To what legal case does Muḥammad compare a successful claim against part of endowed property?
b: The case of a gift (hibah).

f: 101. Why is a successful claim against part of a waqf different from later revocation of part of a gift?
b: Because in the successful claim, joint ownership is treated as existing from the beginning, whereas in revocation it arises only afterward.

f: 102. Why does later revocation of part of a gift not invalidate the original gift?
b: Because the joint ownership arises only after the gift was validly completed.

f: 103. What happens if heirs reclaim two-thirds of property gifted or endowed during terminal illness because the estate is insufficient?
b: The later joint ownership does not invalidate the original transaction.

f: 104. Why does later reclamation by heirs not affect the original validity of a gift or waqf?
b: Because the joint ownership arises only after the original transaction was completed.

f: 105. If the successfully claimed portion is a specifically identified section of the property, what happens to the remainder of the waqf?
b: The waqf of the remaining portion remains valid.

f: 106. Why does a waqf remain valid when the claimed portion is specifically identified?
b: Because no joint ownership exists in the remaining property.

f: 107. Would a waqf over the remaining identified portion have been valid from the outset?
b: Yes.

f: 108. Does the same ruling regarding identified portions apply to gifts and charitable donations that transfer ownership?
b: Yes.

f: 109. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what condition must the ultimate beneficiary of a waqf satisfy?
b: The final destination must be a cause that can never come to an end.

f: 110. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, is a waqf valid if its initial beneficiary will eventually cease to exist?
b: Yes.

f: 111. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what happens after the designated beneficiaries of a waqf cease to exist?
b: The waqf automatically passes to the poor.

f: 112. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, must the poor be expressly mentioned for the waqf to pass to them?
b: No.

f: 113. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad require a perpetual beneficiary for a waqf?
b: Because waqf permanently removes ownership without transferring ownership to another, so its legal effect is inherently perpetual.

f: 114. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, why is a temporary beneficiary inconsistent with waqf?
b: Because a beneficiary that will cease to exist does not fulfill the perpetual nature of waqf.

f: 115. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what is the ruling on limiting a waqf to a fixed period?
b: It is invalid.

f: 116. What analogy do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad use for a time-limited waqf?
b: A sale that is limited to a fixed period.

f: 117. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what is the essential objective of a waqf?
b: Drawing near to Allah.

f: 118. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, does it matter whether the initial beneficiary is temporary or perpetual?
b: No. The objective of seeking closeness to Allah is fulfilled in either case.

f: 119. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why is a waqf to a temporary class of beneficiaries still valid?
b: Because the act of devotion is achieved regardless of whether the beneficiaries eventually cease to exist.

f: 120. What did some scholars say about perpetuity as a condition of waqf?
b: They said everyone agrees that perpetuity is required; the disagreement is only whether it must be expressly stated.

f: 121. According to some scholars, what is the real disagreement between Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and the other two Imams?
b: Whether perpetuity must be explicitly mentioned in the waqf declaration.

f: 122. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why does perpetuity not need to be expressly stated?
b: Because the terms "waqf" and "charitable endowment (ṣadaqah)" inherently indicate perpetuity.

f: 123. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what legal meaning do the words "waqf" and "ṣadaqah" themselves convey?
b: Permanent removal of ownership without transferring ownership to another.

f: 124. To what institution does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله compare the permanence of waqf?
b: Emancipation.

f: 125. According to the text, what happens if a waqf's beneficiaries disappear and no later beneficiaries were specified?
b: It automatically passes to the poor.

f: 126. Why does the text state that the waqf passes to the poor even if they were not mentioned?
b: Because, according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, perpetuity is implied by the very concept of waqf.

f: 127. According to Imām Muḥammad, must a waqf declaration expressly mention perpetual duration?
b: Yes. A waqf declaration must explicitly mention perpetuity.

f: 128. Why does Imām Muḥammad require a waqf declaration to expressly mention perpetuity?
b: Because a donation of usufruct or income may be either temporary or perpetual, so unrestricted wording does not necessarily indicate permanence.

f: 129. According to Imām Muḥammad, why does unrestricted wording not automatically establish a perpetual waqf?
b: Because such wording can refer to either a temporary or a perpetual donation of usufruct or income.

f: 130. Is it permissible to establish a waqf over immovable property (real estate)?
b: Yes. Establishing a waqf over real estate is permissible.

f: 131. What evidence supports the permissibility of establishing a waqf over real estate?
b: Many of the Companions (رضي الله عنهم) established waqfs of real property.

f: 132. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, is it permissible to establish a waqf over movable property independently?
b: No. Independent waqf of movable property is not permissible according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله.

f: 133. Whose opinion is represented by the statement, "It is not permissible to establish a waqf over movable property"?
b: It represents the opinion of Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله.

f: 134. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, when may movable property be included in a waqf?
b: When it accompanies endowed real estate and serves its intended purpose.

f: 135. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, is it valid to endow cattle together with an endowed estate?
b: Yes. Cattle may be endowed together with the estate.

f: 136. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, is it valid to endow slave tenant farmers together with an endowed estate?
b: Yes. Slave tenant farmers may be included with the endowed estate.

f: 137. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, may equipment used to maintain or guard endowed land be included in the waqf?
b: Yes. Equipment necessary for maintaining or guarding the land may accompany the waqf.

f: 138. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله allow movable property to accompany endowed real estate in a waqf?
b: Because those movable items help achieve the purpose for which the land is endowed.

f: 139. What legal principle does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله use to justify including movable property with endowed real estate?
b: Legal rulings may extend to dependent items even when those rulings would not apply to them independently.

f: 140. What example illustrates the principle that legal rulings may extend to dependent items?
b: Water rights pass as an incident of the sale of land.

f: 141. What example from waqf law illustrates that dependent items may share the ruling of the principal property?
b: Buildings remain part of a waqf together with the land.

f: 142. Does Imām Muḥammad agree that movable property accompanying endowed real estate may be included in the waqf?
b: Yes. He agrees with Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله on this point.

f: 143. Why is Imām Muḥammad's agreement regarding movable property accompanying real estate especially consistent with his legal views?
b: Because he even permits certain movable property to be endowed independently.

f: 144. According to Imām Muḥammad, which movable items may be independently established as a waqf?
b: Horses and weapons.

f: 145. According to Imām Muḥammad, for what purpose may horses and weapons be endowed?
b: They may be endowed for the sake of Allah to be used in jihād.

f: 146. Does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله agree that horses and weapons may be independently endowed as waqf?
b: Yes. He agrees with this ruling.

f: 147. Is the permissibility of endowing horses and weapons based on qiyās or istiḥsān?
b: It is based on istiḥsān (juristic preference).

f: 148. According to strict analogical reasoning (qiyās), would independently endowing horses and weapons be permissible?
b: No. According to qiyās, it would not be permissible.

f: 149. Why is qiyās abandoned in favor of istiḥsān regarding the waqf of horses and weapons?
b: Because authentic narrations establish an exception permitting them.

f: 150. Which ḥadīth is used as evidence for the permissibility of endowing horses and weapons?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "As for Khālid, he has endowed his coats of mail and his horses in the path of Allah."

f: 151. Which Companion is mentioned in the ḥadīth as having endowed coats of mail and horses for the sake of Allah?
b: Khālid ibn al-Walīd (رضي الله عنه).

f: 152. Which Companion is reported to have endowed his armor for the sake of Allah?
b: Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbaydillāh (رضي الله عنه).

f: 153. According to another narration, what did Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbaydillāh endow?
b: He endowed his horses.

f: 154. In the narrations about waqf, what does the word kurāʿ mean?
b: It refers to horses.

f: 155. Are camels included in the ruling permitting the endowment of military equipment?
b: Yes. Camels are included in the same ruling.

f: 156. Why are camels included in the ruling permitting the endowment of military equipment?
b: Because the Arabs also fought using camels.

f: 157. According to another narration from Imām Muḥammad, which movable property may be established as a waqf?
b: Any movable property that people customarily endow may be established as a waqf.

f: 158. According to Imām Muḥammad, why may any customarily endowed movable property be made into a waqf?
b: Because widespread custom (ta'āmul) can justify departing from analogy (qiyās).

f: 159. According to Imām Muḥammad, what is the legal basis for permitting the waqf of customarily endowed movable property?
b: Widespread commercial custom (ta'āmul).

f: 160. According to Imām Muḥammad, can widespread custom (ta'āmul) justify abandoning qiyās?
b: Yes. Widespread custom can justify abandoning qiyās.

f: 161. Which legal contract does Imām Muḥammad cite as an example of abandoning qiyās due to widespread custom?
b: The contract of manufacture (istiṣnāʿ).

f: 162. According to Imām Muḥammad, may axes be established as a waqf?
b: Yes, if they are among the movable items customarily endowed by people.

f: 163. According to Imām Muḥammad, may spades be established as a waqf?
b: Yes, if they are customarily endowed.

f: 164. According to Imām Muḥammad, may adzes be established as a waqf?
b: Yes, if they are customarily endowed.

f: 165. According to Imām Muḥammad, may saws be established as a waqf?
b: Yes, if they are customarily endowed.

f: 166. According to Imām Muḥammad, may funeral biers and their shrouds be established as a waqf?
b: Yes, if they are customarily endowed.

f: 167. According to Imām Muḥammad, may cooking pots and cauldrons be established as a waqf?
b: Yes, if they are customarily endowed.

f: 168. According to Imām Muḥammad, may copies of the Qur'an be established as a waqf?
b: Yes. Copies of the Qur'an may be endowed.

f: 169. Did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله agree that any customarily endowed movable property may be made into a waqf?
b: No. He limited the exception to items supported by explicit textual evidence.

f: 170. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why may only certain movable items be established as a waqf?
b: Because exceptions to qiyās should be limited to cases established by explicit texts.

f: 171. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, which movable items are explicitly supported by textual evidence for waqf?
b: Horses and weapons.

f: 172. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why should the exception permitting movable waqf remain limited to horses and weapons?
b: Because the textual evidence mentions only horses and weapons.

f: 173. According to Imām Muḥammad, why may customarily endowed movable property be treated like horses and weapons?
b: Because widespread custom, like explicit text, can justify departing from qiyās.

f: 174. Who is reported to have endowed his books by analogy with copies of the Qur'an?
b: Naṣīr ibn Yaḥyā.

f: 175. Why did Naṣīr ibn Yaḥyā consider it valid to endow books by analogy with copies of the Qur'an?
b: Because both are preserved for the sake of religion through teaching, learning, or recitation.

f: 176. Why is the analogy between books and copies of the Qur'an considered sound?
b: Because both serve the preservation and transmission of religion.

f: 177. Which opinion regarding movable waqf was adopted by the majority of the jurists of the major cities?
b: Imām Muḥammad's opinion permitting movable property customarily endowed by people.

f: 178. According to the majority of jurists, may movable property customarily endowed by people be established as a waqf?
b: Yes.

f: 179. According to Imām Muḥammad's view, may movable property for which no established custom of endowment exists be made into a waqf?
b: No. Such movable property may not be endowed.

f: 180. According to al-Shāfiʿī, what kinds of property may be established as a waqf?
b: Any property whose benefit can be enjoyed while its substance remains intact and which may lawfully be sold.

f: 181. According to al-Shāfiʿī, why may any durable, saleable property be established as a waqf?
b: Because it resembles real estate, horses, and weapons in that its benefit continues while the object remains.

f: 182. How do the Ḥanafīs respond to al-Shāfiʿī's argument permitting all durable movable property as waqf?
b: They argue that such an endowment is not necessarily perpetual, and perpetuity is an essential condition of waqf.

f: 183. Why do the Ḥanafīs reject making all durable movable property into a waqf?
b: Because such property does not necessarily satisfy the requirement of perpetuity.

f: 184. According to the Ḥanafīs, what essential condition of waqf is lacking in most movable property?
b: Perpetuity.

f: 185. According to the Ḥanafīs, what do ordinary movable goods resemble more than real estate regarding waqf?
b: They resemble dirhams and dinars.

f: 186. According to the Ḥanafīs, why does the original qiyās remain applicable to most movable property?
b: Because there is neither explicit textual evidence nor established custom supporting an exception.

f: 187. Why is real estate treated differently from ordinary movable property in the law of waqf?
b: Because real estate naturally endures and thus fulfills the requirement of perpetuity.

f: 188. Why are horses and weapons given a special ruling in the law of waqf according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because jihād occupies a uniquely high rank in religion, making their devotional significance especially strong.

f: 189. According to the Ḥanafīs, why can ordinary movable property not simply be treated like real estate, horses, and weapons in waqf?
b: Because those categories possess special characteristics—natural permanence or explicit religious significance—not shared by ordinary movable goods.

f: 190. Once a waqf is valid, may it be sold?
b: No. A valid waqf may not be sold.

f: 191. Once a waqf is valid, may its ownership be transferred to another person?
b: No. A valid waqf may not be transferred into another person's ownership.

f: 192. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what is the exception to the rule that a waqf cannot be transferred?
b: An undivided share in jointly owned property may be partitioned if the co-owner demands partition.

f: 193. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, when is partition of a waqf's undivided share in jointly owned property permissible?
b: When the co-owner demands partition.

f: 194. Why is partition of a waqf permissible according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله even though ownership cannot be transferred?
b: Because partition is primarily regarded as separating and identifying shares rather than transferring ownership.

f: 195. Why is partition of waqf property not treated as a sale?
b: Because its predominant legal character is the separation of shares, not an exchange of ownership.

f: 196. Who carries out the partition if a person endows his undivided share of jointly owned real estate?
b: The endower carries out the partition with his co-owner.

f: 197. After the death of the endower, who has authority to partition an undivided waqf share with the co-owner?
b: The endower's executor.

f: 198. Who carries out the partition if a person endows one-half of property that he previously owned entirely?
b: The judge carries out the partition.

f: 199. Why does the judge perform the partition when a person endows one-half of property he previously owned entirely?
b: Because the same individual cannot simultaneously act as both parties to the partition.

f: 200. How may an endower arrange the partition of one-half of property he previously owned entirely without the judge directly partitioning it?
b: He may sell the remaining half to another person, allow that purchaser to partition with the waqf, and later buy the sold half back.

f: 201. Why can the owner not personally partition property after endowing one-half of property he previously owned entirely?
b: Because one person cannot simultaneously represent both sides of the partition.

f: 202. What is the ruling if a waqf must pay an equalizing cash adjustment during partition?
b: The partition is invalid because that would amount to selling part of the waqf.

f: 203. Why is partition invalid if the waqf must pay an equalizing cash adjustment?
b: Because a waqf cannot lawfully be sold.

f: 204. What is the ruling if an equalizing cash adjustment is paid to the waqf during partition?
b: The partition is valid.

f: 205. How is a cash adjustment paid to a waqf during partition legally classified?
b: It is treated as an ordinary purchase rather than part of the partition itself.

f: 206. Before distributing the income of a waqf, what must it first be used for?
b: Maintaining and repairing the waqf property.

f: 207. Must the income of a waqf be used for repairs even if the endower did not explicitly stipulate this?
b: Yes. Repair and maintenance are required even without an explicit condition.

f: 208. Why must the income of a waqf first be used to maintain the waqf property?
b: Because preserving the property is necessary for the waqf to continue benefiting its beneficiaries perpetually.

f: 209. Why is a condition requiring maintenance considered implied in every waqf?
b: Because perpetual benefit cannot continue unless the property itself is preserved.

f: 210. Which legal maxim supports using waqf income for maintenance before distribution?
b: Al-kharāj bi'l-ḍamān (benefit accompanies responsibility).

f: 211. What example is given to illustrate the principle that expenses follow responsibility?
b: The maintenance of a slave whose services have been bequeathed is borne by the person entitled to those services.

f: 212. If a waqf is dedicated to the poor in general, who bears the cost of repairing the waqf?
b: The repairs are paid from the waqf's own income.

f: 213. Why are repairs paid from the waqf's income when the waqf is dedicated to the poor?
b: Because no specific individual can be required to bear the expense.

f: 214. If a waqf is dedicated to a specific individual during his lifetime and then to the poor afterward, who pays for repairs?
b: The specific beneficiary pays from his own wealth.

f: 215. From which property must the lifetime beneficiary pay for repairs to a waqf?
b: From whichever of his own assets he chooses.

f: 216. Why is nothing deducted from the waqf's income when the waqf is dedicated to a specific beneficiary?
b: Because there is an identified individual who can legally be required to bear the expense.

f: 217. To what extent is a specific beneficiary required to maintain a waqf?
b: He must restore it to the condition in which it was originally endowed.

f: 218. Why must the beneficiary restore the waqf only to its original condition?
b: Because the income was dedicated based on the property existing in that original state.

f: 219. Is a beneficiary required to improve a waqf beyond its original condition?
b: No. He is only required to restore it, not improve it.

f: 220. Why is a beneficiary not required to improve a waqf beyond its original condition?
b: Because the waqf's income already belongs to the beneficiary and cannot be diverted elsewhere without his consent.

f: 221. When a waqf is dedicated to the poor, what did some jurists permit regarding improvements?
b: They permitted using the waqf's income for improvements beyond ordinary repairs.

f: 222. What is the sounder opinion regarding using the income of a waqf dedicated to the poor for improvements?
b: It may only be used for necessary repairs, not additional improvements.

f: 223. Why is using waqf income for ordinary repairs permitted?
b: Because preserving the waqf is a necessity.

f: 224. Why is using waqf income for improvements beyond ordinary repairs not permitted according to the sounder opinion?
b: Because there is no necessity requiring such improvements.

f: 225. If a house is endowed as a waqf for the residence of the endower's children, who is responsible for its maintenance?
b: Those entitled to live in the house are responsible for its maintenance.

f: 226. Why are the beneficiaries of a residential waqf responsible for its maintenance?
b: Because liability for expenses follows the benefit derived from the property (al-kharāj bi'l-ḍamān).

f: 227. Which legal principle explains why the residents of a residential waqf must pay for repairs?
b: The principle that liability for expenses accompanies the benefit derived from the property (al-kharāj bi'l-ḍamān).

f: 228. What example is used to illustrate the rule that maintenance follows the benefit received from a waqf?
b: The case of a slave whose services have been bequeathed, where the beneficiary bears the maintenance costs.

f: 229. What should the judge do if the beneficiary of a residential waqf refuses to repair the property?
b: The judge rents out the property, pays for repairs from the rental income, and then returns possession to the beneficiary.

f: 230. What should the judge do if the beneficiary of a residential waqf cannot afford the repairs?
b: The judge rents out the property, repairs it using the rental income, and afterward restores possession to the beneficiary.

f: 231. Why does the judge rent out a residential waqf when the beneficiary cannot or will not repair it?
b: To preserve both the waqf itself and the beneficiary's right of residence.

f: 232. Which two rights are protected when the judge rents out a residential waqf to finance repairs?
b: The endower's right that the waqf be preserved and the beneficiary's right of residence.

f: 233. Why does preserving the waqf take priority when repairs are needed?
b: Because without repairs the beneficiary's right of residence would eventually disappear altogether.

f: 234. Can a beneficiary of a residential waqf be compelled to spend his own money on repairs?
b: No.

f: 235. Why can the beneficiary of a residential waqf not be compelled to pay for repairs from his own wealth?
b: Because forcing him to do so would compel him to dispose of his own property.

f: 236. Which legal analogy is used to show that a beneficiary cannot be forced to pay for repairs?
b: The case of sharecropping (muzāraʿah), where the owner of the seed cannot be compelled to provide it.

f: 237. Does refusing to repair a residential waqf amount to forfeiting the beneficiary's right of residence?
b: No. His refusal does not amount to relinquishing his right.

f: 238. Why does refusing to repair a residential waqf not cancel the beneficiary's right of residence?
b: Because the situation may later change, allowing him to benefit again.

f: 239. May the beneficiary of a residential waqf lease the property to someone else?
b: No.

f: 240. Why may the beneficiary of a residential waqf not lease the property?
b: Because he is not its owner.

f: 241. What should be done with the remaining building materials from a ruined waqf if repairs are immediately needed?
b: They should be used immediately to repair the waqf.

f: 242. What should be done with the remaining building materials from a ruined waqf if no repairs are presently needed?
b: They should be kept until repairs become necessary.

f: 243. Why should the remaining materials of a ruined waqf be preserved if there is no immediate need for repairs?
b: So they will be available when repairs are needed in the future.

f: 244. Why must the remaining materials of a ruined waqf be used for repairs?
b: Because preserving the waqf fulfills the endower's intention of making the waqf perpetual.

f: 245. What should be done if the original building materials of a ruined waqf cannot practically be reused?
b: They should be sold, and the proceeds spent on repairing the waqf.

f: 246. Why are the proceeds from selling unusable waqf materials spent on repairs?
b: Because the substitute (their value) takes the same legal ruling as the original materials.

f: 247. May the demolished materials of a ruined waqf be distributed among the beneficiaries?
b: No.

f: 248. Why may the demolished materials of a waqf not be distributed among the beneficiaries?
b: Because they remain part of the corpus of the waqf.

f: 249. What rights do the beneficiaries of a waqf have regarding the waqf property?
b: They have rights only to its usufruct and income, not to its corpus.

f: 250. Why do the beneficiaries of a waqf have no right to the corpus of the waqf?
b: Because the corpus belongs to Allah and cannot be distributed beyond the rights granted by the waqf.

f: 251. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, may an endower stipulate that the income of his waqf belongs to himself?
b: Yes. Such a stipulation is valid according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله.

f: 252. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, may an endower appoint himself as the administrator of his waqf?
b: Yes. He may appoint himself as the administrator.

f: 253. What are the two separate issues discussed regarding an endower's conditions in a waqf?
b: (1) Reserving the income of the waqf for himself, and (2) reserving the administration of the waqf for himself.

f: 254. According to Muḥammad, is it valid for an endower to reserve the income of his waqf for himself?
b: No. It is not valid according to Muḥammad.

f: 255. Which scholars agreed with Muḥammad that reserving the income of a waqf for oneself is invalid?
b: Hilāl al-Rāzī and al-Shāfiʿī.

f: 256. According to some jurists, what earlier disagreement explains the dispute over reserving waqf income for oneself?
b: The earlier disagreement over whether delivery and separation of the property are conditions for the validity of a waqf.

f: 257. According to other jurists, is the issue of reserving waqf income for oneself dependent upon the disagreement over delivery and possession?
b: No. They regarded it as an independent legal issue.

f: 258. Does the disagreement about reserving waqf income apply only when all the income is reserved for the endower?
b: No. It applies whether he reserves all or only part of the income for himself.

f: 259. Does the disagreement about reserving waqf income apply when the endower reserves the income for himself only during his lifetime and then dedicates it to the poor?
b: Yes.

f: 260. If an endower reserves all the income of a waqf for himself during his lifetime and then dedicates it to the poor afterward, is this subject to the same juristic disagreement?
b: Yes.

f: 261. If an endower reserves the income of a waqf for his umm walad slave-concubines during his lifetime and then for the poor, is this subject to juristic disagreement?
b: According to the sounder opinion, yes.

f: 262. If an endower reserves the income of a waqf for his mudabbar slaves during his lifetime and then for the poor, is this subject to juristic disagreement?
b: According to the sounder opinion, yes.

f: 263. Why is reserving the income of a waqf for an umm walad or mudabbar slave treated like reserving it for oneself?
b: Because benefiting them during the endower's lifetime is legally equivalent to benefiting himself.

f: 264. Why does Muḥammad consider reserving waqf income for oneself invalid?
b: Because waqf is an act of charity that transfers rights, and reserving its benefit for oneself defeats that transfer.

f: 265. According to Muḥammad, why can an endower not reserve the benefit of a waqf for himself?
b: Because a person cannot transfer ownership or rights to himself.

f: 266. To what does Muḥammad compare reserving waqf income for oneself?
b: To making a charitable donation while retaining it for oneself or reserving part of a mosque for private use.

f: 267. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what ḥadīth supports the validity of reserving waqf income for oneself?
b: The report that the Prophet ﷺ used to eat from his own charity.

f: 268. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what is meant by the report that the Prophet ﷺ ate from his own charity?
b: It refers to his charitable endowment (waqf).

f: 269. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why does the Prophet's ﷺ eating from his own waqf support the validity of reserving waqf income?
b: Because such use would only have been lawful if it had been stipulated.

f: 270. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what happens to ownership when a valid waqf is established?
b: Ownership leaves the donor and becomes dedicated to Allah.

f: 271. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why is reserving the benefit of a waqf for oneself permissible?
b: Because the donor is benefiting from property dedicated to Allah, not from property he still owns.

f: 272. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, is benefiting from a waqf after reserving its income equivalent to making one's own property belong to oneself?
b: No. The property already belongs to Allah, and the donor merely benefits from it.

f: 273. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what examples illustrate the permissibility of reserving benefit from property dedicated to Allah?
b: Building a caravanserai, a public drinking fountain, or a cemetery while stipulating that the donor may benefit from it.

f: 274. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, may the founder of a caravanserai stipulate that he may stay there?
b: Yes.

f: 275. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, may the founder of a public drinking fountain stipulate that he may drink from it?
b: Yes.

f: 276. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, may the founder of a cemetery stipulate that he may be buried there?
b: Yes.

f: 277. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why does reserving personal benefit from a waqf not contradict its devotional nature?
b: Because the donor's objective remains drawing near to Allah, and benefiting oneself from charitable property is permissible.

f: 278. What ḥadīth does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله cite to support the permissibility of reserving benefit from one's own waqf?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "A man's spending on himself is charity."

f: 279. According to the ḥadīth cited by Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, is spending on oneself considered an act of charity?
b: Yes. The Prophet ﷺ said, "A man's spending on himself is charity."

f: 280. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, may an endower stipulate that he can exchange the waqf property for another parcel of land whenever he wishes?
b: Yes. Both the waqf and this condition are valid according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله.

f: 281. According to Muḥammad, what is the ruling if an endower stipulates that he may exchange the waqf property for another parcel of land whenever he wishes?
b: The waqf remains valid, but the condition is void.

f: 282. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, may an endower reserve a three-day option (khiyār) to revoke the waqf?
b: Yes. Both the waqf and the condition are valid.

f: 283. According to Muḥammad, what is the ruling if an endower reserves a three-day option (khiyār) to revoke the waqf?
b: The waqf itself is invalid.

f: 284. Upon what underlying disagreement are the rulings concerning exchanging waqf property and reserving a three-day option based?
b: They are based on the earlier disagreement between Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding the legal nature and completion of waqf.

f: 285. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, may an endower appoint himself as the administrator (nāẓir) of his own waqf?
b: Yes.

f: 286. Which scholars agreed with Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله that an endower may appoint himself as the administrator of his waqf?
b: Hilāl and the apparent position of the Ḥanafī school.

f: 287. According to the view attributed by the Ḥanafīs to Muḥammad, when does an endower retain the right to administer his waqf?
b: Only if he expressly reserves administration for himself.

f: 288. According to the view attributed to Muḥammad, what happens if an endower does not expressly reserve administration of his waqf?
b: He has no authority to administer it.

f: 289. Why does the view attributed to Muḥammad deny administrative authority to the endower unless he expressly reserves it?
b: Because Muḥammad considers delivery of the waqf to an administrator a condition for its validity, after which the donor no longer has authority over it.

f: 290. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why may an endower appoint himself as administrator of his waqf?
b: Because the administrator's authority comes from the donor's appointment, so it would be contradictory for the donor himself to lack that authority.

f: 291. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, why is the donor the person most entitled to administer his own waqf?
b: Because he has the closest legal relationship to the waqf.

f: 292. What analogy does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله use to show that the donor has the strongest claim to administer a waqf?
b: The founder of a mosque has the strongest claim to supervise it and appoint its mu'adhdhin.

f: 293. What second analogy does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله use to support the donor's right to administer a waqf?
b: The emancipator acquires the right of walāʾ because of his close legal relationship to the freed slave.

f: 294. May a judge remove an endower from administering his waqf if the endower proves untrustworthy?
b: Yes.

f: 295. Why may a judge remove an endower from administering his own waqf?
b: To protect the interests of the poor and preserve the waqf.

f: 296. What legal analogy supports removing an untrustworthy administrator of a waqf?
b: The removal of an executor in order to protect orphaned minors.

f: 297. Is a condition valid that prohibits the ruler or judge from ever removing the endower as administrator of the waqf?
b: No. Such a condition is invalid.

f: 298. Why is a condition preventing the judge from removing the administrator of a waqf invalid?
b: Because it contradicts the rulings of the Sharīʿah.

f: 299. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, when does ownership cease after a person builds a mosque?
b: After it is separated from his property, opened to the public for prayer, and at least one person prays in it.

f: 300. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what two conditions must be fulfilled before ownership of a newly built mosque ceases?
b: It must be physically separated from the owner's property, and prayer must actually be performed in it.

f: 301. Why must a mosque be physically separated from the owner's remaining property before it becomes a mosque?
b: Because it cannot become exclusively dedicated to Allah unless it is distinguished from the owner's property.

f: 302. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, why must prayer actually be performed in a newly built mosque?
b: Because delivery (taslīm) is a condition for completing its dedication.

f: 303. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, what constitutes the proper form of delivery (taslīm) for a mosque?
b: That prayer is actually performed in it.

f: 304. Why does actual prayer take the place of physical delivery in the dedication of a mosque?
b: Because physical delivery of a mosque is impossible, so realization of its intended purpose substitutes for delivery.

f: 305. According to one narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, how many people must pray in a newly built mosque for the dedication to be completed?
b: The prayer of a single person is sufficient.

f: 306. According to one narration from Muḥammad, how many people must pray in a newly built mosque for the dedication to be completed?
b: The prayer of a single person is sufficient.

f: 307. Why is the prayer of a single person sufficient according to one narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: Because requiring every potential worshipper to pray there is impossible, so the minimum realization of the mosque's purpose is enough.

f: 308. According to another narration from Muḥammad, what kind of prayer is required before a newly built mosque is fully dedicated?
b: Congregational prayer.

f: 309. Why does another narration from Muḥammad require congregational prayer before a mosque is fully dedicated?
b: Because a mosque is ordinarily established for congregational worship.

f: 310. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, when does ownership leave a person who dedicates a building as a mosque?
b: Ownership ceases immediately upon the donor's declaration, "I have made it a mosque," because delivery is not a condition according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله.

f: 311. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله hold that ownership of a mosque ends immediately upon declaration?
b: Because dedicating a mosque consists of relinquishing human ownership, and once ownership is abandoned the property becomes exclusively devoted to Allah, analogous to emancipation.

f: 312. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, when does ownership cease after establishing a mosque?
b: Ownership ceases only after the mosque is separated from the donor's property and prayer is performed in it.

f: 313. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, why must a mosque be separated from the donor's remaining property?
b: So that it becomes exclusively devoted to Allah and is no longer connected to the donor's private ownership.

f: 314. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, why is prayer in the mosque required before ownership ceases?
b: Because delivery (taslīm) is a condition for completing the dedication, and prayer is the appropriate form of delivery for a mosque.

f: 315. According to one narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, how much prayer is sufficient to complete the dedication of a mosque?
b: The prayer of a single person is sufficient because complete participation by all worshippers is impossible.

f: 316. According to another narration from Muḥammad, what level of prayer is required before a mosque dedication is complete?
b: Congregational prayer, since a mosque is ordinarily established for congregational worship.

f: 317. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the ruling if someone builds a mosque with a cellar beneath it or a room above it while retaining those areas for personal use?
b: The mosque may still be sold, and after the owner's death it passes to his heirs because it has not become exclusively dedicated to Allah.

f: 318. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله invalidate a mosque built with privately owned structures above or below it?
b: Because human rights remain attached to the property, preventing it from becoming exclusively dedicated to Allah.

f: 319. When is a cellar beneath a mosque permissible according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: When the cellar is intended solely for the needs of the mosque.

f: 320. Which famous mosque is cited as an example of a mosque with a permissible cellar?
b: The Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

f: 321. According to al-Ḥasan's narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the ruling if the lower floor is designated as a mosque and the upper floor remains a residence?
b: The lower floor is a valid mosque because perpetuity is realized there even if not in the upper floor.

f: 322. According to Muḥammad, is a mosque valid if there is a residence above it?
b: No. He held that such an arrangement compromises the honor and reverence due to a mosque.

f: 323. Why did Muḥammad object to having residential or commercial premises above a mosque?
b: Because it diminishes the dignity and sanctity that a mosque should possess.

f: 324. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله later permit mosques with residences above or below them?
b: Because of necessity arising from the scarcity of housing after he arrived in Baghdad.

f: 325. Why did Muḥammad later permit mosques with residences above or below them?
b: Because of necessity after observing housing shortages in Rayy.

f: 326. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what is the ruling if someone converts the middle portion of his house into a mosque while retaining ownership of the surrounding house?
b: It may still be sold and inherited because it has not become a true mosque.

f: 327. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله hold that a mosque inside a privately owned house is not a true mosque?
b: Because the owner still has the right to exclude people by controlling access through his private property.

f: 328. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, why does a mosque inside a private house fail to become exclusively dedicated to Allah?
b: Because the owner retains the access route and therefore retains private rights over the property.

f: 329. According to Muḥammad, what is the ruling on a mosque established inside the middle of a private house?
b: It becomes a true mosque and may neither be sold, inherited, nor gifted.

f: 330. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, does a mosque established inside the middle of a private house become a true mosque?
b: Yes. Once the owner declares it to be a mosque, it becomes a mosque.

f: 331. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله consider a mosque inside a private house valid?
b: Because the right of public access is implied by the dedication itself, just as rights necessary for the use of leased property are implied even if not expressly mentioned.

f: 332. What is the ruling on revoking, selling, or inheriting land that has been validly dedicated as a mosque?
b: The dedication cannot be revoked, the land cannot be sold, and it does not pass to the founder's heirs because it has become exclusively devoted to Allah.

f: 333. Why can land dedicated as a mosque no longer be revoked, sold, or inherited?
b: Because all human rights over it have ceased and it has become exclusively devoted to Allah.

f: 334. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what happens if the area surrounding a mosque falls into ruin and the mosque is no longer needed?
b: It remains a mosque permanently because ownership, once relinquished, can never return.

f: 335. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله maintain that an abandoned mosque remains a mosque?
b: Because the dedication permanently removes ownership, and ownership cannot return after being relinquished.

f: 336. According to Muḥammad, what happens if a mosque is no longer needed because the surrounding area has fallen into ruin?
b: Ownership returns to the builder, or after his death to the builder's heirs.

f: 337. Why does Muḥammad hold that ownership of an abandoned mosque returns to its builder or heirs?
b: Because the property was dedicated for a specific act of worship, and when that purpose ceases, the legal effect of the dedication also ceases.

f: 338. What analogy does Muḥammad use to support the return of ownership when a mosque is no longer needed?
b: He compares it to mosque mats or grass that are no longer needed for the mosque.

f: 339. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what should be done with mosque mats or grass that are no longer needed?
b: They should be transferred to another mosque rather than returned to private ownership.

f: 340. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, when does ownership cease for a public fountain, inn (khān), frontier lodge (ribāṭ), or cemetery dedicated as a waqf?
b: Ownership does not cease until a judge confirms the waqf (or it is made effective upon death).

f: 341. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله require judicial confirmation for a waqf of a fountain, inn, ribāṭ, or cemetery?
b: Because the founder still retains personal rights to benefit from these endowments.

f: 342. What personal benefits may the founder continue to enjoy from a public fountain, inn, ribāṭ, or cemetery according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: He may drink from the fountain, stay in the inn, reside in the ribāṭ, or be buried in the cemetery.

f: 343. Why is a mosque treated differently from a fountain, inn, ribāṭ, or cemetery according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because the founder retains no personal right to benefit from a mosque, making it exclusively devoted to Allah.

f: 344. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, when does ownership cease for a fountain, inn, ribāṭ, or cemetery dedicated as a waqf?
b: Ownership ceases immediately upon the declaration of the waqf.

f: 345. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله hold that ownership of a fountain, inn, ribāṭ, or cemetery ends immediately upon declaration?
b: Because delivery is not a condition for the validity of a waqf according to him.

f: 346. According to Muḥammad, when does ownership cease for a fountain, inn, ribāṭ, or cemetery dedicated as a waqf?
b: Ownership ceases once people actually begin using it for its intended purpose.

f: 347. According to Muḥammad, what constitutes delivery for a public fountain?
b: People actually drawing water from it.

f: 348. According to Muḥammad, what constitutes delivery for an endowed inn or ribāṭ?
b: People actually staying in it.

f: 349. According to Muḥammad, what constitutes delivery for an endowed cemetery?
b: People actually burying the dead in it.

f: 350. According to Muḥammad, is the use of a single person sufficient to complete delivery of these endowments?
b: Yes. The use of a single person is sufficient because universal use is impossible.

f: 351. Does the same ruling apply to an endowed well or reservoir according to Muḥammad?
b: Yes. The same rule regarding delivery through public use applies.

f: 352. Is delivery of an endowed fountain, inn, ribāṭ, or cemetery to an appointed administrator (mutawallī) valid?
b: Yes. Delivery to the administrator is valid because the administrator represents the beneficiaries.

f: 353. Why is delivery to the mutawallī considered sufficient for most endowments?
b: Because the mutawallī acts as the legal representative of the beneficiaries, and the representative's act is equivalent to theirs.

f: 354. Is delivery of a mosque to its mutawallī sufficient according to all jurists?
b: No. There are two opinions regarding whether delivery to the mutawallī completes the dedication of a mosque.

f: 355. Why do some jurists say delivery of a mosque to its mutawallī is insufficient?
b: Because the mutawallī has no true authority of administration over the mosque itself.

f: 356. Why do other jurists consider delivery of a mosque to its mutawallī sufficient?
b: Because someone must care for the mosque by cleaning it and locking its doors, making the mutawallī an appropriate recipient of delivery.

f: 357. How do some jurists classify a cemetery regarding delivery to a mutawallī?
b: They treat it like a mosque, since cemeteries ordinarily have no administrator.

f: 358. How do other jurists classify a cemetery regarding delivery to a mutawallī?
b: They treat it like a fountain or an inn, making delivery to the mutawallī valid.

f: 359. Why do some jurists permit delivery of a cemetery to a mutawallī?
b: Because appointing a mutawallī for a cemetery is legally permissible, even if it is not customary.

f: 360. Is it valid to endow a house in Makkah as lodging for pilgrims performing ḥajj or ʿumrah?
b: Yes. Such an endowment is valid and irrevocable.

f: 361. Is it valid to endow a house outside Makkah for the poor?
b: Yes. Such an endowment is valid and irrevocable.

f: 362. Is it valid to endow a house on the frontier as lodging for fighters and frontier guards?
b: Yes. Such an endowment is valid and irrevocable.

f: 363. Is it valid to endow the produce of land for those striving in the path of Allah while appointing a supervisor (mutawallī)?
b: Yes. Such an endowment is valid and irrevocable.

f: 364. Who may benefit from the income or produce of a waqf according to this passage?
b: Only the poor are entitled to benefit from the income or produce of such an endowment.

f: 365. May wealthy people benefit from the income or produce of a charitable waqf?
b: No. The income or produce is intended only for the poor.

f: 366. Who may benefit from a waqf consisting of lodging, water, or similar public facilities?
b: Both the rich and the poor may benefit equally.

f: 367. May wealthy people stay in an endowed inn or draw water from an endowed fountain?
b: Yes. Public utility endowments are available to both rich and poor alike.

f: 368. Why are the beneficiaries of income endowments restricted to the poor?
b: Because customary understanding treats income-producing charitable endowments as being intended for the poor.

f: 369. Why may both rich and poor benefit from endowed lodging, wells, and fountains?
b: Because customary understanding treats such public facilities as being available equally to everyone.

f: 370. What is the juristic basis for distinguishing between income endowments and public utility endowments?
b: The distinction is based on customary understanding (ʿurf).

f: 371. Why are wealthy people excluded from receiving the income of a waqf but not from using its public facilities?
b: Because wealthy people do not ordinarily need financial support, whereas both rich and poor need water and temporary lodging.

f: 1. How is a sale concluded according to the Ḥanafī jurists?
b: A sale is concluded through offer (ījāb) and acceptance (qabūl) expressed in the past tense.

f: 2. Give an example of valid wording for offer and acceptance in a sale.
b: One party says, "I have sold," and the other replies, "I have purchased."

f: 3. Why is a sale valid when offer and acceptance are expressed in the past tense?
b: Because the Sharīʿah has designated words originally intended to report past events as valid forms for creating legal transactions.

f: 4. Is a sale valid if one party uses the future tense while the other uses the past tense?
b: No. A sale is not concluded when one party uses the future tense and the other uses the past tense.

f: 5. Why does the rule regarding the future tense in sales differ from the rule in marriage?
b: Because marriage has a distinct legal basis already explained in the chapter on marriage.

f: 6. Do expressions other than "I have sold" and "I have bought" conclude a sale?
b: Yes. Expressions that convey the same meaning also conclude a sale.

f: 7. Does saying, "I am pleased with this for such-and-such," conclude a valid sale?
b: Yes, because it conveys the legal meaning of sale.

f: 8. Does saying, "I have given it to you for such-and-such," conclude a valid sale?
b: Yes, because it conveys the legal meaning of sale.

f: 9. Does saying, "Take it for such-and-such," conclude a valid sale?
b: Yes, because it conveys the legal meaning of sale.

f: 10. Why are different expressions capable of concluding a sale?
b: Because in sales the legally significant factor is the intended meaning, not the specific wording.

f: 11. Is a sale by mutual exchange without spoken words (taʿāṭī) valid?
b: Yes. According to the preferred opinion, a sale by mutual exchange is valid because it demonstrates mutual consent.

f: 12. Does the validity of taʿāṭī depend on whether the item is valuable or insignificant?
b: No. It is valid regardless of the value of the item.

f: 13. What is khiyār al-qabūl (the option of acceptance)?
b: It is the right of the offeree to either accept or reject the offer during the same contractual session.

f: 14. Why is the offeree given the option of acceptance?
b: So that the legal consequences of the sale do not become binding without his consent.

f: 15. May the offeror withdraw his offer before it is accepted?
b: Yes. Since the sale is incomplete until acceptance, the offeror may revoke the offer before acceptance.

f: 16. Why is the offeror allowed to withdraw the offer before acceptance?
b: Because no rights of the other party have yet become established.

f: 17. How long does the option of acceptance remain in effect?
b: Until the end of the contractual session (majlis).

f: 18. Why does the option of acceptance continue throughout the contractual session?
b: Because the Sharīʿah treats all moments within one sitting as though they were one continuous moment, making transactions easier.

f: 19. Does a written offer have the same legal effect as a spoken offer?
b: Yes. A written offer has the same legal effect as a spoken offer.

f: 20. Does an offer delivered through a messenger have the same legal effect as a spoken offer?
b: Yes. An offer sent by messenger has the same legal effect as a spoken offer.

f: 21. In the case of a written offer, when does the contractual session begin?
b: When the written offer reaches the recipient.

f: 22. In the case of an offer sent by messenger, when does the contractual session begin?
