f: 377. According to the preferred Ḥanafī explanation, when does an option period exceeding three days actually invalidate the contract?
b: Only when part of the fourth day has elapsed while the excessive option condition still remains.

f: 378. What is the other reported explanation regarding a sale with an option period exceeding three days?
b: That the contract is invalid from the outset but becomes valid once the excessive condition is removed.

f: 379. Which explanation regarding an excessive option period is preferred in the Ḥanafī school?
b: The preferred explanation is that the contract only becomes invalid once part of the fourth day has elapsed.

f: 380. If someone buys on condition that if he does not pay the price within three days there is no sale, is the condition valid?
b: Yes. According to all three Imāms, the condition is valid if the period is three days. If payment is made within those three days, the sale is valid.

f: 381. If the period for the "no payment, no sale" condition is four days, what is the ruling according to the three Imāms?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, the sale is invalid. According to Muḥammad, it is valid even if the period is four days or longer, provided it is specified.

f: 382. Why is the condition "if I do not pay within three days, there is no sale" treated like an option (khiyār al-sharṭ)?
b: Because it serves the same purpose as an option: allowing the sale to terminate if payment is not made, thereby protecting the seller from delay.

f: 383. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله invalidate a payment-condition period exceeding three days?
b: Because he treats it like a stipulated option, and in his view an option may not exceed three days.

f: 384. Why does Muḥammad allow the payment-condition period to exceed three days?
b: Because he consistently permits stipulated options for any specified period, and this condition has the same legal effect as an option.

f: 385. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله differ between the original option issue and the payment-condition issue?
b: In the original issue he follows the transmitted report permitting only the established ruling, whereas in this issue he follows analogy (qiyās).

f: 386. What is Zufar's analogy regarding the payment-condition clause?
b: He regards it as a sale containing a conditional rescission (iqālah). Since even a valid rescission made conditional invalidates the sale, an invalid conditional rescission should invalidate it even more.

f: 387. Why is Zufar's analogy not adopted by the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because they prefer juristic preference (istiḥsān), treating the clause as analogous to a valid option due to practical need.

f: 388. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, what effect does the seller's option have on ownership of the sold item?
b: The sold item remains in the seller's ownership until the option period ends or the sale is confirmed.

f: 389. Why does the seller retain ownership while he has the option?
b: Because complete mutual consent has not yet been established, so the sale is not fully completed.

f: 390. If a seller emancipates a slave during the seller's option period, is the emancipation valid?
b: Yes. Since ownership has not left the seller, the emancipation takes effect.

f: 391. During the seller's option period, may the buyer dispose of the purchased item after taking possession?
b: No. The buyer may not dispose of it even if the seller permitted him to take possession.

f: 392. If the buyer possesses the item and it perishes during the seller's option period, what is he liable for?
b: He must pay its market value, because the sale is annulled by the destruction of the subject matter and his possession is treated as possession for the purpose of purchase (qabd ʿalā sawm al-shirāʾ).

f: 393. If the sold item perishes while still with the seller during the seller's option period, what happens?
b: The sale simply ends, and the buyer bears no liability.

f: 394. Does the buyer's option prevent the sold item from leaving the seller's ownership?
b: No. The property leaves the seller's ownership even though the buyer has the option.

f: 395. Why does the buyer's option not prevent the property from leaving the seller's ownership?
b: Because the sale is binding with respect to the seller, and the option exists only for the buyer's benefit.

f: 396. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, does the buyer become the owner while he has the option?
b: No. The property leaves the seller's ownership but does not yet enter the buyer's ownership.

f: 397. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, does the buyer become the owner during his option period?
b: Yes. Ownership transfers to the buyer immediately despite his option.

f: 398. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad say ownership transfers immediately during the buyer's option?
b: Because property cannot exist without an owner, so once it leaves the seller's ownership it must enter the buyer's ownership.

f: 399. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله deny that the buyer becomes the owner during his option period?
b: Because the purchase price still belongs to the buyer. If ownership of the item also transferred, both counter-values would belong to one person, contrary to the nature of a contract of exchange.

f: 400. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله use the example of purchasing a close relative to support his view?
b: If ownership transferred immediately, a purchased slave who was a close relative would become automatically free, depriving the buyer of the benefit of the option period that was legislated for his protection.

f: 401. If the purchased item perishes while in the buyer's possession during the buyer's option (khiyār al-sharṭ), what is the ruling?
b: The item is lost in exchange for the agreed purchase price, so the buyer must pay the price.

f: 402. If the purchased item develops a defect while in the buyer's possession during the buyer's option, what is the ruling?
b: The buyer must pay the agreed purchase price because the defect prevents him from returning the item.

f: 403. Why is the buyer liable for the price if the item is destroyed or becomes defective during the buyer's option?
b: Because the contract has already become binding in this respect, and a defect prevents the item from being returned. Destruction is treated as the ultimate form of defect.

f: 404. Why is the ruling different when the seller possesses the option?
b: Because a defect does not prevent the seller from rescinding the sale. Therefore, if the item perishes, the suspended sale is simply annulled rather than completed.

f: 405. Is a sale conducted by a blind person valid?
b: Yes. The sale and purchase of a blind person are valid.

f: 406. Does a blind buyer have the option of inspection (khiyār al-ruʾyah)?
b: Yes. Since he purchases something he has not seen, he possesses the option of inspection.

f: 407. How does a blind buyer waive the option of inspection for items whose qualities are known by touch?
b: By feeling the item.

f: 408. How does a blind buyer waive the option of inspection for items known by smell?
b: By smelling the item.

f: 409. How does a blind buyer waive the option of inspection for items known by taste?
b: By tasting the item.

f: 410. How is the option of inspection waived for a blind buyer purchasing real estate?
b: It is waived only after the property is described to him, because the description takes the place of seeing it.

f: 411. Why is a description sufficient for a blind buyer purchasing real estate?
b: Because a description substitutes for seeing, just as it does in a salam (forward sale) contract.

f: 412. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله view regarding a blind buyer's inspection of real estate?
b: If he stands where a sighted person could have seen the property and then says, "I am satisfied," his option is waived.

f: 413. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله consider standing in the viewing position sufficient for a blind buyer?
b: Because where the actual act is impossible, the closest equivalent is treated as taking its place.

f: 414. What was al-Ḥasan's opinion regarding how a blind buyer should inspect purchased property?
b: He should appoint an agent to inspect and take possession on his behalf.

f: 415. Why did al-Ḥasan recommend appointing an agent for a blind buyer?
b: Because the agent's inspection is legally treated as the inspection of the principal.

f: 416. If someone sees one of two garments before purchasing both, then later sees the second garment, what right does he have?
b: He has the option to return both garments.

f: 417. Why does seeing one of two garments not remove the option of inspection for both?
b: Because seeing one garment does not amount to seeing the other, as garments may differ in quality.

f: 418. May the buyer return only the garment he had not previously seen?
b: No. He must either keep both or return both.

f: 419. Why may the buyer not return only one of the two garments?
b: Because this would divide the transaction before it has become complete.

f: 420. While the option of inspection remains, is the sale regarded as complete?
b: No. The sale is not regarded as complete until the option of inspection ends.

f: 421. Does the buyer need the seller's consent or a judge's ruling to rescind a sale under the option of inspection?
b: No. The buyer may rescind the sale without either the seller's consent or a judge's ruling.

f: 422. When a buyer rescinds under the option of inspection, from when does the rescission take effect?
b: It takes effect retroactively from the beginning of the contract.

f: 423. If a person dies while possessing the option of inspection (khiyār al-ruʾyah), does the option pass to his heirs?
b: No. The option of inspection is extinguished upon his death and is not inherited.

f: 424. Why is the option of inspection not inherited?
b: Because, according to the Ḥanafīs, it is a personal right that does not pass to heirs, just like the option of stipulation (khiyār al-sharṭ).

f: 425. If someone previously inspected an item and later purchases it while it remains unchanged, does he have the option of inspection?
b: No. Since he already knows its qualities from the earlier inspection, he has no option.

f: 426. Why does a previous inspection remove the option of inspection?
b: Because the purpose of the option is to remove ignorance of the item's qualities, and that knowledge has already been obtained.

f: 427. If an item has changed since the buyer last saw it, does he have the option of inspection?
b: Yes. The earlier inspection no longer reflects the item's present condition, so he has the option.

f: 428. Why does a change in the item's condition restore the option of inspection?
b: Because the previous inspection no longer provides reliable knowledge of the item's current qualities.

f: 429. If the buyer and seller disagree over whether the purchased item has changed since it was last seen, whose statement is accepted?
b: The seller's statement is accepted because the original presumption is that the sale remains binding, and change is something occurring later that must be proven.

f: 430. When might the buyer's claim that the item has changed be preferred?
b: If a long period has passed, the apparent circumstances support the likelihood that the item has changed.

f: 431. If the parties dispute whether the buyer had ever previously seen the item, whose statement is accepted?
b: The buyer's statement is accepted, because prior inspection is an event that requires proof, and he denies that it occurred.

f: 432. If someone buys a bale of cloth without inspecting it, then sells or gives away one garment from it and delivers it, may he later rescind the purchase under the option of inspection?
b: No. He may not return the remainder under the option of inspection. He may only return it if a defect is discovered.

f: 433. Why does disposing of one garment prevent rescission under the option of inspection?
b: Because the garment that left his ownership cannot be returned, and returning only the remainder would improperly divide the transaction before it is complete.

f: 434. Does the same ruling apply to the option of stipulation (khiyār al-sharṭ)?
b: Yes. Disposing of part of the purchased goods likewise prevents rescission under the option of stipulation.

f: 435. Why is the option for defect (khiyār al-ʿayb) treated differently from the option of inspection and the option of stipulation?
b: Because the sale is considered complete after possession despite the existence of the option for defect, whereas the options of inspection and stipulation prevent the sale from becoming fully complete.

f: 436. If a garment that the buyer disposed of later returns to him through a transaction amounting to rescission, does the option of inspection revive according to al-Sarakhsī?
b: Yes. According to Shams al-Aʾimmah al-Sarakhsī, the option of inspection returns.

f: 437. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, does the option of inspection revive if the garment returns to the buyer?
b: No. Once the option has lapsed, it does not revive, just as the option of stipulation does not revive.

f: 438. Which opinion regarding the revival of the option of inspection was preferred by al-Qudūrī?
b: He preferred the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله that the option does not revive once it has lapsed.

f: 439. If a buyer discovers a defect in the purchased item, what options does he have?
b: He may either keep the item for the full agreed price or return it and rescind the sale.

f: 440. Why does a buyer have the option of rescission when a defect is discovered?
b: Because an unrestricted sale implicitly requires the item to be free from defects, and the buyer did not consent to purchase a defective item.

f: 441. May a buyer keep a defective item and demand compensation for the reduction in its value?
b: No. He must either keep it for the full price or return it.

f: 442. Why may the buyer not keep a defective item and reduce the purchase price?
b: Because descriptive qualities are not assigned a separate portion of the price, and the seller did not consent to sell the item for less than the agreed amount.

f: 443. Why does Islamic law give the buyer only the choice of rescission instead of a price reduction?
b: Because this removes the buyer's harm without imposing an unagreed loss upon the seller.

f: 444. Under what conditions does the option for defect (khiyār al-ʿayb) arise?
b: The defect must have existed while the item was in the seller's possession, and the buyer must have been unaware of it both at the time of the sale and at the time of taking possession.

f: 445. If the buyer knew of the defect before purchasing or before taking possession, does he retain the option for defect?
b: No. His knowledge and acceptance amount to approval of the defect.

f: 446. How is a legal defect defined in the Ḥanafī school?
b: Anything that merchants customarily regard as reducing the market value of the item is considered a defect.

f: 447. Why is the custom of merchants used to determine whether something is a defect?
b: Because the legal harm lies in the reduction of the item's market value, and merchants are the standard for assessing that value.

f: 448. Are running away, bed-wetting, and stealing considered defects in a child?
b: Yes, so long as the child has not reached maturity.

f: 449. After puberty, are running away, bed-wetting, and stealing automatically treated as the same defects that existed in childhood?
b: No. They are not treated as the same defect unless they recur after puberty.

f: 450. If a child displayed one of these defects while with the seller and it recurs while he is still a child in the buyer's possession, may the buyer return him?
b: Yes. It is regarded as the continuation of the same defect.

f: 451. If running away, bed-wetting, or stealing first appears only after puberty, may the buyer return the slave on that basis?
b: No. These are regarded as different conditions with different underlying causes.

f: 452. Why is bed-wetting before puberty treated differently from bed-wetting after puberty?
b: Because in childhood it is attributed to weakness of the bladder, whereas after puberty it indicates an internal illness.

f: 453. Why is running away before puberty treated differently from running away after puberty?
b: Because in childhood it usually results from a love of play, whereas after puberty it indicates corruption of character.

f: 454. Why is stealing before puberty treated differently from stealing after puberty?
b: Because in childhood it arises from immaturity and lack of understanding, whereas after puberty it indicates corruption of character.

f: 455. Which type of child is intended in the discussion of childhood defects such as running away?
b: A child who has reached the age of understanding (mumayyiz).

f: 456. Is a child who has not yet reached the age of understanding considered a runaway slave if he wanders away?
b: No. He is regarded merely as lost (ḍāll), so this is not considered a legal defect.

f: 457. If insanity first occurs during childhood while the slave is with the seller, and it later recurs while with the buyer, may the buyer return the slave?
b: Yes. If the insanity recurs while the slave is in the buyer's possession—whether during childhood or after adulthood—the buyer may rescind the sale.

f: 458. Why does insanity that begins in childhood remain a defect even if it recurs after adulthood?
b: Because it is regarded as the same underlying illness whose cause, an internal disorder, remains the same before and after maturity.

f: 459. Must insanity actually recur while the buyer owns the slave before he may rescind the sale?
b: Yes. Even if the slave had previously been insane, the defect must reappear during the buyer's ownership before rescission is permitted.

f: 460. Why is the buyer not entitled to rescind merely because the slave was once insane in the seller's possession?
b: Because the illness may have completely disappeared, and the buyer may rescind only if the defect actually exists again during his ownership.

f: 461. Are bad breath and offensive body odour considered defects in a female slave?
b: Yes. They are considered defects because they interfere with the intended purposes of sexual relations and childbearing.

f: 462. Why are bad breath and offensive body odour defects in a female slave?
b: Because they diminish the intended benefit of purchasing her for intimacy and having children.

f: 463. Are bad breath and offensive body odour considered defects in a male slave?
b: No. They are not ordinarily defects because they do not normally interfere with the intended purpose of service.

f: 464. When does offensive body odour become a defect even in a male slave?
b: When it results from an illness, because illness itself is a legal defect.

f: 465. Is fornication considered a defect in a female slave?
b: Yes. It is regarded as a defect because it undermines the intended purposes of sexual relations and childbearing.

f: 466. Is being born through fornication considered a defect in a female slave?
b: Yes. It is regarded as a defect for the same reason.

f: 467. Is fornication considered a defect in a male slave?
b: Not ordinarily. Since the intended purpose of purchasing a male slave is service, fornication does not normally affect that purpose.

f: 468. When does fornication become a defect in a male slave?
b: When it becomes a habitual practice that interferes with his ability to perform his duties and provide service.

f: 469. If a buyer discovers a qualifying defect in the purchased item, what choices does he have?
b: He may either keep the item for the full agreed price or return it and rescind the sale.

f: 470. Why does discovering a defect give the buyer the option of rescission?
b: Because an unrestricted sale implicitly requires the item to be sound, and the buyer did not consent to purchase a defective item.

f: 471. May the buyer keep the defective item and demand compensation (arsh) for the reduction in value?
b: No. He must either keep it for the full agreed price or return it.

f: 472. Why is the buyer not entitled to compensation (arsh) while keeping the item?
b: Because qualities are not assigned a separate portion of the contract price, and the seller did not agree to sell for less than the stipulated amount.

f: 473. What type of defect gives rise to the option for defect (khiyār al-ʿayb)?
b: A defect that existed while the item was in the seller's possession and of which the buyer was unaware at the time of sale and at the time of taking possession.

f: 474. If the buyer knew of the defect before the sale or before taking possession, may he later rescind on that basis?
b: No. His knowledge of the defect is treated as acceptance of it.

f: 475. How is a legal defect (ʿayb) generally defined in the Ḥanafī school?
b: Anything that merchants customarily regard as reducing the market value of an item is considered a legal defect.

f: 476. Why is merchant custom used to determine whether something is a defect?
b: Because the relevant legal harm is the reduction in the item's market value, and merchants determine what affects that value.

f: 477. Are running away, bedwetting, and theft considered defects in a minor slave?
b: Yes. They are defects so long as the slave has not reached puberty.

f: 478. If running away, bedwetting, or theft appears while the slave is a minor with the seller and recurs while he is still a minor with the buyer, may the buyer return him?
b: Yes. The recurrence is treated as the continuation of the same defect.

f: 479. If running away, bedwetting, or theft first appears only after the slave reaches puberty, may the buyer return him?
b: No. These are regarded as different defects because their causes after puberty differ from those in childhood.

f: 480. Why is bedwetting before puberty treated differently from bedwetting after puberty?
b: Because in childhood it is attributed to weakness of the bladder, whereas after puberty it indicates an internal illness.

f: 481. Why is running away before puberty treated differently from running away after puberty?
b: Because in childhood it is due to a love of play, whereas after puberty it indicates corruption of character.

f: 482. Why is theft before puberty treated differently from theft after puberty?
b: Because in childhood it results from lack of restraint or immaturity, whereas after puberty it reflects corrupt character.

f: 483. Which type of minor is intended in the discussion of defects such as running away?
b: A minor who has reached the age of discernment (mumayyiz).

f: 484. Is a child who has not reached the age of discernment considered a runaway if he wanders away?
b: No. He is regarded merely as lost, so this is not considered a legal defect.

f: 485. If insanity first appears during childhood while the slave is with the seller and later recurs while with the buyer, may the buyer return him?
b: Yes. If the insanity recurs during the buyer's ownership, whether before or after puberty, the buyer may rescind the sale.

f: 486. Why is insanity that begins in childhood treated as the same defect even after puberty?
b: Because it is regarded as the same underlying illness arising from the same internal cause.

f: 487. Must insanity actually recur while the buyer owns the slave before the buyer may rescind the sale?
b: Yes. The defect must reappear during the buyer's ownership before the right of return arises.

f: 488. Why is recurrence of insanity required before the buyer may rescind the sale?
b: Because the illness may have completely disappeared, and rescission is only justified if the defect actually exists during the buyer's ownership.

f: 489. Are bad breath and offensive body odor considered defects in a female slave?
b: Yes. They are considered defects because they interfere with the intended purposes of intimacy and childbearing.

f: 490. Why are bad breath and offensive body odor defects in a female slave?
b: Because they diminish the intended benefits for which a female slave may be purchased.

f: 491. Are bad breath and offensive body odor ordinarily defects in a male slave?
b: No. They are not ordinarily defects because they do not interfere with the intended purpose of service.

f: 492. When do bad breath and offensive body odor become defects in a male slave?
b: When they result from an illness, because illness itself is a legal defect.

f: 493. What is the ruling if a female slave is found to have committed fornication or to have been born out of wedlock?
b: Both are defects in a female slave because they interfere with the intended purposes of intimacy and childbearing, giving the buyer the option of rescission.

f: 494. Are fornication and illegitimate birth considered defects in a male slave?
b: No. They are not defects because they do not normally interfere with the primary purpose of purchasing a male slave, which is service.

f: 495. When does fornication become a defect in a male slave?
b: If fornication becomes his habitual practice, it is considered a defect because constantly pursuing women interferes with his usefulness in service.

f: 496. Why is habitual fornication treated differently from occasional fornication in a male slave?
b: Because habitual misconduct affects his ability to perform his duties, whereas occasional fornication does not ordinarily impair his usefulness.

f: 497. Is disbelief (kufr) considered a defect in a slave?
b: Yes. Disbelief is a defect in both male and female slaves according to the Ḥanafīs.

f: 498. Why is disbelief regarded as a defect in a slave?
b: Because Muslims naturally dislike close companionship with a disbeliever, and a disbelieving slave cannot be used for certain acts of expiation (kaffārāt), reducing his value.

f: 499. If a buyer purchases a slave believing him to be a disbeliever but later discovers he is a Muslim, may the buyer rescind the sale?
b: No. The buyer has no right to rescind because the supposed defect has been removed rather than established.

f: 500. What was al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding buying a slave believed to be a disbeliever but later found to be Muslim?
b: He held that the buyer may rescind because the failure of a stipulated quality gives rise to the option of rescission, even if the substitute quality is generally better.

f: 501. When is the absence of menstruation considered a defect in a female slave?
b: When she has reached the maximum age of puberty according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله (seventeen years) and still does not menstruate, since this indicates illness.

f: 502. Is continuous abnormal bleeding (istiḥāḍah) a defect in a female slave?
b: Yes. It is regarded as a defect because it is a sign of illness.

f: 503. How is the absence of menstruation established in a dispute?
b: It is established by the slave woman's own statement, provided the seller refuses to swear an oath denying it.

f: 504. Does the ruling regarding proof of absent menstruation differ before and after delivery?
b: No. According to the sound opinion, the same rule applies both before and after delivery.

f: 505. What happens if the buyer discovers an old defect after a new defect has arisen while the item is in his possession?
b: He may recover compensation (arsh) for the original defect but may not return the item.

f: 506. Why may the buyer not return an item that developed a new defect while in his possession?
b: Because returning it would unfairly harm the seller by restoring property burdened with a defect that was not present when it left the seller's ownership.

f: 507. When may the buyer return an item despite a new defect arising in his possession?
b: If the seller voluntarily agrees to accept it back despite the new defect.

f: 508. If a buyer cuts a garment and then discovers a pre-existing defect, may he return it?
b: No. Cutting the garment is itself a new defect that prevents return, but he may claim compensation for the original defect.

f: 509. Why does cutting a garment prevent its return for a pre-existing defect?
b: Because cutting constitutes a new defect that would prejudice the seller if the garment were returned.

f: 510. Can the seller still accept back a cut garment?
b: Yes. If the seller willingly accepts it in that condition, he may do so because the prohibition on return exists for his benefit and he may waive it.

f: 511. What happens if the buyer sells the garment after discovering the defect?
b: He loses the right to compensation because he has made return impossible by his own act after the seller was willing to accept it back.

f: 512. Why does selling the defective garment extinguish the buyer's right to compensation?
b: Because once the seller agrees to accept its return, the buyer himself becomes responsible for making return impossible by disposing of the garment.

f: 513. What is the ruling if the buyer cuts and sews a garment, dyes it red, or mixes roasted flour (sawīq) with butter, then discovers a pre-existing defect?
b: He may not return the item but is entitled to compensation (arsh) for the defect.

f: 514. Why does adding an inseparable improvement to the purchased item prevent its return?
b: Because the sale cannot be rescinded without the inseparable increase, and it cannot be rescinded together with it since the increase was never part of the original sale.

f: 515. Why does the buyer receive compensation instead of rescinding the sale after making an inseparable improvement?
b: Because rescission has become legally impossible, leaving compensation as the only remedy.

f: 516. Can the seller insist on taking back an item that has received an inseparable increase?
b: No. The seller has no right to reclaim it because the obstacle to rescission arises by operation of Sharīʿah, not merely for the seller's personal benefit.

f: 517. If the buyer sells an item after discovering its defect, having already made an inseparable improvement to it, may he still recover compensation?
b: Yes. Since rescission was already impossible before the sale, the later sale does not deprive him of his right to compensation.

f: 518. Why does selling the improved item after discovering the defect not prevent compensation?
b: Because the impossibility of rescission already existed before the buyer sold it.

f: 519. If a buyer makes cloth into clothing for his minor child before discovering a defect, may he recover compensation?
b: No. Ownership passed to the minor child before the sewing occurred, preventing the buyer from claiming compensation.

f: 520. Why can the buyer not claim compensation when he sews the cloth into clothing for his minor child?
b: Because ownership transferred to the child before the inseparable improvement was made.

f: 521. If the buyer makes cloth into clothing for his adult child before discovering a defect, may he recover compensation?
b: Yes. Ownership passes to an adult child only upon delivery, so the sewing occurred while the buyer still owned the cloth.

f: 522. Why may the buyer recover compensation when sewing clothing for his adult child?
b: Because the inseparable improvement occurred before ownership passed to the adult child.

f: 523. What is the ruling if the buyer emancipates a slave and only afterwards discovers a pre-existing defect?
b: He may recover compensation (arsh) for the defect according to istiḥsān.

f: 524. What is the ruling if the purchased slave dies before the buyer discovers a pre-existing defect?
b: The buyer may recover compensation for the defect.

f: 525. Why does the buyer receive compensation if the slave dies before the defect is discovered?
b: Because return became impossible by operation of law through death, not through the buyer's own act.

f: 526. According to strict analogy (qiyās), should a buyer who emancipates a defective slave receive compensation?
b: No. Qiyās would deny compensation because the buyer himself made return impossible by emancipating the slave.

f: 527. Why does istiḥsān allow compensation after emancipation?
b: Because emancipation is regarded as the natural completion of ownership, making it analogous to the termination of ownership through death.

f: 528. Why is emancipation viewed as the completion of ownership?
b: Because human beings were not originally created to remain property, and ownership over them is regarded as temporary until emancipation.

f: 529. How does the law treat ownership when a slave is emancipated before a defect is discovered?
b: It treats ownership as though it continued until return became legally impossible, allowing compensation.

f: 530. Do the rulings on compensation after emancipation also apply to tadbīr and istīlād?
b: Yes. Both are treated similarly because legal impediments prevent transferring the slave while the person still physically exists.

f: 531. What is the ruling if the buyer emancipates the slave in exchange for payment and later discovers a defect?
b: He is not entitled to compensation according to the main narration.

f: 532. Why is compensation denied when emancipation occurs in exchange for payment?
b: Because the buyer retained a substitute value, and keeping the substitute is treated as equivalent to retaining the original property.

f: 533. Is there another narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله regarding emancipation for payment?
b: Yes. Another narration states that the buyer may still recover compensation because emancipation still terminates ownership, even when it is for consideration.

f: 534. What is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله if the buyer kills a purchased slave and later discovers a pre-existing defect?
b: He has no right to compensation (arsh).

f: 535. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله deny compensation when the buyer kills the purchased slave?
b: Because return became impossible through an act that ordinarily entails liability, even though liability is waived here due to ownership.

f: 536. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding a buyer who kills a defective slave before discovering the defect?
b: He held that the buyer may still recover compensation because a master incurs no worldly liability for killing his own slave, making it analogous to natural death.

f: 537. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish killing a slave from emancipating him?
b: Because killing ordinarily gives rise to liability, whereas emancipation does not inherently entail liability.

f: 538. What is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله if the buyer consumes purchased food before discovering a pre-existing defect?
b: He has no right to compensation.

f: 539. What is the ruling according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad if the buyer consumes purchased food before discovering a pre-existing defect?
b: They held that the buyer may recover compensation for the defect.

f: 540. Does the same disagreement apply if the buyer wears a garment until it becomes worn out before discovering a defect?
b: Yes. The same disagreement between Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and the two disciples applies.

f: 541. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad allow compensation after food is consumed or clothing is worn out?
b: Because the buyer merely used the item for its intended purpose, similar to emancipating a slave.

f: 542. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله deny compensation after food is consumed or clothing is worn out?
b: Because return became impossible through an act for which the buyer would ordinarily be liable regarding the property, making it analogous to selling or destroying it.

f: 543. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله reject the argument that consuming or using the item was its intended purpose?
b: Because selling is also a normal exercise of ownership, yet it likewise prevents recovery of compensation.

f: 544. What is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله if only part of the purchased food is consumed before discovering the defect?
b: He still denies compensation because food is treated as a single whole.

f: 545. What is the ruling according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad if only part of the purchased food is consumed before discovering the defect?
b: They allow the buyer to recover compensation for the defect affecting the whole item.

f: 546. Is there another narration from the two disciples regarding partial consumption of food?
b: Yes. Another narration states that the buyer may return the remaining portion because partial return does not cause undue harm.

f: 547. What is the ruling if someone buys eggs, melons, cucumbers, gourds, or walnuts, breaks them open, and finds them completely spoiled?
b: He recovers the entire purchase price because the goods have no financial value and the sale is void.

f: 548. Why does a buyer recover the full price when such goods are completely spoiled?
b: Because the goods are entirely without value, making the sale void.

f: 549. In the case of walnuts, what determines whether they are defective?
b: The condition of the kernel, not the shell, because the kernel is what has financial value.

f: 550. What is the ruling if the purchased produce is spoiled but still usable after being opened?
b: The buyer may not return it but may recover compensation for the deficiency.

f: 551. Why may the buyer not return produce that remains usable after being opened?
b: Because opening it creates a new defect that prevents return.

f: 552. Why is compensation allowed when the produce remains usable but spoiled?
b: Because compensation removes the buyer's loss as far as possible when rescission is no longer available.

f: 553. What was al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding opening produce that turns out to be spoiled?
b: He held that the buyer may return it because the seller implicitly permitted opening it.

f: 554. How do the Ḥanafīs answer al-Shāfiʿī's argument regarding opening the produce?
b: They say the seller only permitted opening it while it belonged to the buyer, not while it remained the seller's property, making it analogous to cutting a purchased garment.

f: 555. What is the ruling if only a small portion of the purchased produce is spoiled?
b: The sale remains valid by istiḥsān because a small amount of spoilage is customary and unavoidable.

f: 556. What is considered a "small amount" of spoilage?
b: The amount customarily expected, such as one or two spoiled walnuts out of a hundred.

f: 557. What is the ruling if a large proportion of the purchased produce is spoiled?
b: The sale is invalid, and the buyer recovers the full purchase price.

f: 558. Why is a sale invalid when a large proportion of the produce is spoiled?
b: Because the sale effectively combines valuable property with something that has no value, similar to selling a free person together with a slave.

f: 559. If part of the purchased property is lawfully evicted (istihqāq) after the buyer has taken possession, may he return the remainder?
b: No. He has no option to return what remains.

f: 560. Why does lawful eviction of part of the purchased property after possession not give the buyer the right to rescind the remainder?
b: Because the division does not legally harm him through splitting the sale, and eviction by a third party does not prevent the completion of the contract, which depends only on the consent of the contracting parties.

f: 561. If lawful eviction of part of the purchased property occurs before possession, may the buyer rescind the remainder?
b: Yes. He may return what remains because the sale has been divided before becoming complete.

f: 562. Why does lawful eviction before possession allow rescission of the remainder?
b: Because the sale is divided before its completion, giving the buyer the option to rescind.

f: 563. Does the ruling on lawful eviction differ between garments and fungible goods?
b: Yes. A garment is treated differently because division of a garment itself constitutes a defect.

f: 564. If part of a purchased garment is lawfully evicted, does the buyer have the option to rescind?
b: Yes. He has the option because partial loss of a garment is treated as a defect existing from the time of sale.

f: 565. Why does partial lawful eviction of a garment give the buyer an option to rescind?
b: Because dividing a garment diminishes it as an item, unlike fungible goods sold by weight or measure.

f: 566. Why are fungible goods sold by weight or measure treated differently from garments in cases of partial lawful eviction?
b: Because removing part of fungible goods does not create the same kind of defect as dividing a garment.

f: 567. If the buyer treats a wound on a purchased slave-girl before discovering a defect, what does this indicate?
b: It constitutes acceptance (riḍā) of the purchase.

f: 568. If the buyer rides a purchased animal for his own needs before discovering a defect, does this affect his right to rescind?
b: Yes. Riding it for his own benefit constitutes acceptance of the sale.

f: 569. Why does treating a slave-girl's wound or riding an animal for personal benefit amount to acceptance?
b: Because such actions indicate an intention to retain the purchased item.

f: 570. Why does riding an animal not waive the option in Khiyār al-Sharṭ?
b: Because the option by stipulation exists specifically to allow testing and examination of the purchased property.

f: 571. Does riding an animal in order to return it to the seller amount to acceptance?
b: No. It does not, because it is itself part of the process of rescission.

f: 572. Does riding an animal to water it or obtain fodder necessarily amount to acceptance?
b: No. It does not if riding is reasonably necessary and no practical alternative exists.

f: 573. When is riding an animal to water it or obtain fodder not regarded as acceptance?
b: When the buyer has no reasonable alternative, such as if the animal is difficult to lead, the buyer is unable to walk it, or the fodder can only conveniently be carried while riding.

f: 574. If the buyer could reasonably avoid riding the animal but chooses to ride it anyway, what is the ruling?
b: Riding it constitutes acceptance of the sale.

f: 575. If a buyer unknowingly purchases a slave who had previously committed theft and the slave's hand is amputated while in the buyer's possession, what is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله ruling?
b: The buyer may return the slave and recover the full purchase price.

f: 576. What is the ruling of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad if a purchased slave's hand is amputated because of a theft committed before the sale?
b: The buyer recovers only the difference between the slave's value as a thief and his value as a non-thief.

f: 577. Does the same disagreement apply if the slave is executed for an offence committed while in the seller's possession?
b: Yes. The same disagreement applies.

f: 578. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله classify amputation or execution resulting from an offence committed before the sale?
b: He treats it like lawful eviction (istihqāq) by a third party.

f: 579. How do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad classify amputation or execution resulting from an offence committed before the sale?
b: They treat it as an ordinary defect rather than lawful eviction.

f: 580. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad allow only compensation rather than rescission in this case?
b: Because they regard the prior offence merely as the cause of the later punishment, not something that destroyed the slave's value at the time of sale.

f: 581. What analogy do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad use to support their position?
b: They compare it to purchasing a pregnant slave-girl who dies in childbirth, where the buyer recovers only the difference in value.

f: 582. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله allow rescission when the slave's hand is amputated or he is executed for a prior offence?
b: Because the legal cause of the punishment existed while the slave was in the seller's possession, and legal causes are attributed to their consequences.

f: 583. What analogy does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله use to support his reasoning?
b: He compares it to usurped property whose destruction or injury is legally attributed to the earlier wrongful act committed while it was in the usurper's possession.

f: 584. Does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله accept the analogy of the pregnant slave-girl who dies in childbirth?
b: No. He rejects that analogy.

f: 585. If a slave steals once while in the seller's possession and again while in the purchaser's possession, and his hand is amputated for both thefts, what is the ruling according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: The purchaser may not return the slave without the seller's consent because a new defect arose while the slave was in the purchaser's possession. Instead, he recovers one-quarter of the purchase price.

f: 586. Why may the purchaser not return the slave according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله when the slave committed theft both before and after the sale?
b: Because the second theft and resulting amputation occurred while the slave was in the purchaser's possession, creating a new defect attributable to the purchaser's ownership.

f: 587. Why does the purchaser recover one-quarter of the purchase price according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله in this case?
b: Because one hand represents half of a person's value, and that loss occurred through two offences. Only one of those offences gives the purchaser a right of recourse against the seller, so he recovers half of half the value.

f: 588. If the seller agrees to accept the slave back after both thefts and amputation, how much does the purchaser recover according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: He recovers three-quarters of the purchase price.

f: 589. Why does the purchaser recover three-quarters of the price if the seller accepts the slave back?
b: Because the seller's consent removes the obstacle to return, allowing the purchaser to recover for both the seller-related defect and the inability to return due to the later defect.

f: 590. If a slave passes through several owners before his hand is amputated in the possession of the final owner, what is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله ruling?
b: Each seller has recourse against his own seller, similar to cases of lawful eviction (istihqāq).

f: 591. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله allow each seller to seek compensation from his own seller in a chain of sales?
b: Because he treats the punishment as connected to a cause that existed before the transfer, making it analogous to eviction.

f: 592. What is the ruling of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad when a slave passes through multiple owners before amputation?
b: Only the final purchaser may seek compensation from his immediate seller, and that seller has no claim against the seller before him.

f: 593. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad restrict recourse to the final purchaser and immediate seller?
b: Because they classify the matter as a defect rather than lawful eviction, and defects only give the direct purchaser a claim against his seller.

f: 594. Why are the words "without the purchaser knowing" significant according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: Because knowledge of a defect constitutes acceptance, preventing the purchaser from later claiming compensation or rescission.

f: 595. Do the words "without the purchaser knowing" have significance according to Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله strongest opinion?
b: No. Knowledge of a reason for lawful eviction does not prevent the purchaser from exercising his right of recourse.

f: 596. What is the ruling if the seller stipulates that he is free from every defect in the item sold?
b: The purchaser may not return the item for any defect, even if the individual defects were not specified.

f: 597. Why did al-Shāfiʿī consider a general disclaimer of defects invalid?
b: Because he holds that releasing unknown rights is invalid, comparing a release (ibrāʾ) to a transfer of ownership where unknown subjects cannot be transferred.

f: 598. What is the Ḥanafī response to al-Shāfiʿī's objection regarding a general disclaimer of defects?
b: They argue that uncertainty in a waiver does not lead to dispute, and since delivery is not required for a release, uncertainty does not invalidate it.

f: 599. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, what defects are covered by the seller's disclaimer of all defects?
b: It covers defects already existing at the time of sale and defects that arise before delivery.

f: 600. According to Muḥammad and Zufar, what defects are covered by the seller's disclaimer?
b: It covers only defects that already exist at the time of the disclaimer.

f: 601. Why does Muḥammad say that the disclaimer only covers existing defects?
b: Because a release can only apply to something that already exists and cannot waive unknown future matters.

f: 602. How does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله respond to Muḥammad's position on future defects before delivery?
b: He argues that the purpose of the clause is to make the sale binding by waiving the buyer's right to require soundness, and this purpose is only achieved if both existing and pre-delivery defects are included.

f: 603. What is the underlying purpose of a seller's disclaimer of defects?
b: To remove the buyer's right to demand that the purchased item possess the normal attribute of soundness and thereby make the sale fully binding.

f: 604. What is the ruling in the Ḥanafī school when one or both counter-values in a sale are unlawful, such as carrion, blood, pork, or wine?
b: The ruling depends on the nature of the unlawful item. Sales involving carrion, blood, or a free person are void (bāṭil), while sales involving wine or pork are invalid (fāsid).

f: 605. Why is a sale involving carrion, blood, or a free person considered void (bāṭil)?
b: Because the essential pillar of sale—exchanging property for property—is absent. These things are not considered property by anyone.

f: 606. Why is a sale involving wine or pork considered invalid (fāsid) rather than void (bāṭil)?
b: Because the essential reality of sale exists: exchange of property for property. Wine and pork are regarded as property by some people, although they are not legally valuable property (māl mutaqawwam).

f: 607. Does a void sale (bāṭil) transfer ownership of the purchased item?
b: No. A void sale produces no ownership whatsoever.

f: 608. If property purchased through a void sale perishes while in the purchaser's possession, what are the two reported opinions regarding the purchaser's liability?
b: One opinion is that the purchaser holds it merely as a trust because the contract has no legal effect and possession occurred with the owner's permission. Another opinion is that he is liable because his position cannot be weaker than one who receives property while contemplating purchase (sawm al-shirāʾ).

f: 609. Which scholars are reported to hold that property obtained through a void sale is merely held as a trust, and which scholars are reported to hold that the purchaser is liable?
b: It has been said that the first opinion is the position of Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, while the second is the position of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad.

f: 610. Does an invalid (fāsid) sale transfer ownership after possession is taken?
b: Yes. An invalid sale transfers ownership once possession occurs, and the purchased item remains guaranteed in the purchaser's possession.

f: 611. What is al-Shāfiʿī's position regarding ownership transfer in an invalid (fāsid) sale?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī disagrees and does not accept that an invalid sale transfers ownership in this manner.

f: 612. Why are sales involving carrion, blood, and a free person void?
b: Because none of these are property capable of being sold, so the essential element of exchanging property for property is absent.

f: 613. How does the ruling differ when wine or pork is exchanged for a debt such as dirhams or dinars versus when it is exchanged for a specific tangible item?
b: If wine or pork is exchanged for money, the sale is void. If exchanged for a specific tangible item, the sale is invalid (fāsid), and ownership of the lawful item given in exchange is acquired.

f: 614. Why is wine considered property (māl) but not valuable property (mutaqawwam)?
b: Because some people recognize it as property, but Islamic law commands that it be degraded rather than honored, preventing it from being treated as legally valuable property.

f: 615. Why does purchasing wine with money result in a void sale, while purchasing a garment with wine results in an invalid sale?
b: When wine is purchased with money, the actual objective is acquiring the wine itself, so the lack of legal value invalidates the transaction. When a garment is purchased with wine, the actual objective is acquiring the garment, and the honor attaches to the garment rather than the wine.

f: 616. In a sale where wine is given as the price for a lawful item, what must the purchaser pay instead of the agreed wine price?
b: The purchaser must pay the value of the lawful item, not the value of the wine.

f: 617. Why is the designation of wine as the price ignored in an invalid barter transaction?
b: Because wine cannot function as a legally valid price. The mention of wine remains ineffective for ownership of the wine, while the lawful item acquired remains recognized.

f: 618. How is a barter transaction where wine is exchanged for a garment treated in Islamic law?
b: It is treated as though the garment was purchased with wine, so ownership of the garment is acquired, but the wine does not become a valid price.

f: 619. What is the ruling of selling an umm al-walad, a mudabbar, or a mukātab according to the Ḥanafī school?
b: Although the text says the sale is defective (fāsid), what is intended is that the sale is void (bāṭil).

f: 620. Why is the sale of an umm al-walad void?
b: Because she has already acquired a right to freedom based on the Prophet's ﷺ statement: "Her child has emancipated her." Selling her would invalidate an established right.

f: 621. Why is the sale of a mudabbar void?
b: Because the cause of emancipation has already come into existence. After the master's death, ownership of the mudabbar is no longer legally possible, so selling him would conflict with his established status.

f: 622. Why is the sale of a mukātab void?
b: Because the mukātab has acquired a binding right over himself against his master through the contract of emancipation. Selling him would nullify that right.

f: 623. Why does establishing ownership through the sale of an umm al-walad, mudabbar, or mukātab invalidate their existing rights?
b: Because sale-based ownership would conflict with and remove the rights to freedom or self-ownership that they already possess.

f: 624. If a mukātab agrees to being sold, what are the reported opinions regarding the validity of the sale?
b: There are two narrations, and the stronger opinion is that the sale is permissible.

f: 625. Which type of mudabbar is being discussed in the ruling about selling a mudabbar?
b: The ruling concerns the absolute mudabbar (al-mudabbar al-muṭlaq), not the conditional mudabbar (al-mudabbar al-muqayyad).

f: 626. What is the disagreement between the Ḥanafīs and al-Shāfiʿī regarding the absolute mudabbar?
b: There is a disagreement regarding the legal status and rulings of the absolute mudabbar, which was previously discussed in the chapter on emancipation.

f: 627. If an umm al-walad or mudabbar dies while in the purchaser's possession after a defective sale, what is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله ruling regarding liability?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله holds that the purchaser bears no liability for their value.

f: 628. If an umm al-walad or mudabbar dies while in the purchaser's possession after a defective sale, what is the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: They hold that the purchaser is liable for their value.

f: 629. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad consider the purchaser liable for an umm al-walad or mudabbar acquired through a defective sale?
b: Because the property was received through a sale transaction, so it should be guaranteed like other property. They also argue that an umm al-walad and mudabbar may be included in a sale together with other property.

f: 630. How do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad distinguish an umm al-walad and mudabbar from a mukātab regarding liability?
b: They argue that the mukātab remains in possession of himself, meaning the purchaser never obtains legal possession over him, and liability depends upon possession.

f: 631. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله response to the argument that an umm al-walad and mudabbar can be included in a sale?
b: He argues that the effects of sale only apply where the reality of sale is legally possible. Since these individuals cannot truly be sold, they resemble the mukātab. Their inclusion only affects accompanying property, not themselves.

f: 632. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله compare the inclusion of an umm al-walad or mudabbar in a sale to the inclusion of a person's own property?
b: Because a person's own property is not truly included in his own sale, but it may be treated as included only because it accompanies other property. Likewise, an umm al-walad or mudabbar is not included for their own sake.

f: 633. What is the ruling on selling fish before they have been caught?
b: It is not permissible because it involves selling property that the seller does not own.

f: 634. Why is selling fish in an enclosure invalid if the fish cannot be taken except by fishing?
b: Because the seller is unable to deliver the fish, and delivery of the sold item is required for a valid sale.

f: 635. What type of fish enclosure is being discussed when saying that fish cannot be sold if they require fishing to remove them?
b: It refers to fish that were first caught and then placed inside an enclosure.

f: 636. When is the sale of fish in an enclosure valid?
b: If the fish can be taken without special effort or fishing, the sale is valid because delivery is possible.

f: 637. Why is the sale of fish invalid if they entered the enclosure by themselves and the entrance was never closed?
b: Because ownership was never established. The seller never acquired possession of the fish, so he cannot sell them.

f: 638. Why is it impermissible to sell birds while they are flying?
b: Because they are not owned before capture, and one cannot sell what one does not own.

f: 639. Why is selling a bird invalid if someone releases it from his hand and then sells it?
b: Because delivery of the bird cannot be guaranteed after it has been released.

f: 640. What is the ruling on selling a fetus or future offspring?
b: It is not permissible because the Prophet ﷺ prohibited the sale of ḥabal and ḥabal al-ḥabalah, and because such sales involve excessive uncertainty (gharar).

f: 641. Why is selling a fetus or future offspring considered invalid?
b: Because the subject matter is uncertain and may not even exist, creating excessive uncertainty in the transaction.

f: 642. Why is selling milk still inside the udder impermissible?
b: Because there is uncertainty regarding whether the swelling is actually milk, how much milk exists, and how the milking will be carried out.

f: 643. What additional uncertainty exists when selling milk inside the udder?
b: New milk may be produced and mix with the sold milk, making it difficult to distinguish what was actually sold.

f: 644. Why is selling wool while it remains on the sheep's back impermissible?
b: Because wool is treated as an attribute of the animal, it continues growing from the base, and the sold wool becomes mixed with newly grown wool.

f: 645. Why is wool on the sheep's back different from the animal's legs regarding growth?
b: Wool grows from the base, causing new growth to mix with the sold portion, whereas the legs increase only from the top.

f: 646. Why is wool on the sheep's back different from green fodder (qaṣīl)?
b: Green fodder can simply be uprooted, whereas wool requires cutting, and disagreement may arise regarding where it should be cut.

f: 647. What Prophetic narration is used as evidence regarding the sale of wool and milk?
b: The Prophet ﷺ prohibited the sale of wool while on the sheep's back, milk in the udder, and butter while still mixed with milk.

f: 648. What position attributed to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله does the narration about wool contradict?
b: It contradicts the narration from Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله in which he permitted selling wool while it remains on the sheep.

f: 649. Why may one not sell a beam fixed in a roof?
b: Because delivery cannot occur without causing damage to the structure.

f: 650. Why may one not sell a cubit of cloth when it requires cutting?
b: Because removing the sold portion causes damage, and delivery cannot occur without harming the original item.

f: 651. Why is selling a portion of a silver lump different from selling a beam or a cubit of cloth?
b: Because dividing silver does not cause damage, whereas removing part of a fixed beam or cloth causes harm.

f: 652. What is the ruling if a beam or cubit of cloth is not specifically identified in the sale?
b: The sale is invalid because of both uncertainty and the inability to deliver the sold item.

f: 653. If the seller cuts off the cubit of cloth or removes the beam before the buyer cancels the sale, does the sale become valid?
b: Yes. The sale becomes valid because the cause of invalidity—impossibility of delivery—has been removed.

f: 654. Why does a sale of a beam or cubit of cloth become valid after removal, while a sale of date pits inside dates does not?
b: Because the beam or cloth portion is an existing identifiable object whose delivery problem was later removed, whereas the existence of date pits or seeds inside fruit was uncertain from the beginning.

f: 655. Why does extracting seeds from a watermelon after the sale not make the sale valid?
b: Because the existence of the seeds was uncertain at the time of the contract, unlike an already existing beam or cloth portion.

f: 656. What is meant by the hunter's strike (ḍarbat al-qāniṣ) in defective sales?
b: It refers to selling whatever game may be caught by a single cast of a hunting net.

f: 657. Why is the hunter's strike (ḍarbat al-qāniṣ) an invalid sale?
b: Because the subject matter is unknown and the transaction contains excessive uncertainty (gharar).

f: 658. What is muzābanah?
b: Muzābanah is selling fruit still on date palms in exchange for harvested dates based on an estimated equivalent measure.

f: 659. Why is muzābanah prohibited?
b: Because it involves exchanging a measured commodity for another commodity of the same type based only on estimation, creating uncertainty.

f: 660. What Prophetic prohibition is cited regarding muzābanah and muḥāqalah?
b: The Prophet ﷺ prohibited muzābanah and muḥāqalah.

f: 661. What is muḥāqalah?
b: Muḥāqalah is selling wheat still in its ears in exchange for harvested wheat according to an estimated equivalent measure.

f: 662. Why is muḥāqalah invalid?
b: Because it involves exchanging wheat for wheat of the same genus based on estimation rather than exact measurement.

f: 663. What other transaction receives the same ruling as muzābanah?
b: Exchanging grapes still on the vine for raisins receives the same ruling.

f: 664. What was al-Shāfiʿī's position regarding muzābanah involving less than five wasqs?
b: He held that it is permissible when the amount is less than five wasqs, based on the concession regarding the ʿarāyā sale.

f: 665. What evidence did al-Shāfiʿī use to permit certain small amounts of muzābanah?
b: He relied on the Prophet's ﷺ concession regarding ʿarāyā, where estimated dates on a tree could be exchanged for harvested dates below five wasqs.

f: 666. How do the Ḥanafīs respond to al-Shāfiʿī's use of the ʿarāyā concession?
b: They explain that ʿariyyah literally means a gift, and the transaction is not truly a sale but a continuation of charity after gifting a palm tree.

f: 667. Why is the ʿarāyā transaction not considered an ordinary sale according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because after gifting the palm tree, the giver no longer owns the dates, so the exchange is treated as a charitable act rather than a normal sale.

f: 668. What were the pre-Islamic sales of mulāmasah, munābadhah, and ilqāʾ al-ḥajar?
b: They were sales where the contract became binding through an uncertain action: touching the item, throwing the item toward the buyer, or throwing a stone onto the goods.

f: 669. Why are sales by touching, throwing, or casting a stone invalid?
b: Because they make the contract dependent upon an uncertain event involving risk and ambiguity.

f: 670. Which forms of pre-Islamic sale did the Prophet ﷺ prohibit?
b: He prohibited sales by touching (mulāmasah) and throwing (munābadhah).

f: 671. Why is it invalid to sell "one cloth out of two" without further specification?
b: Because the subject matter of the sale is unknown.

f: 672. When is selling one cloth out of two valid?
b: It is valid if the buyer is given the option to choose whichever of the two cloths he wishes, according to juristic preference (istiḥsān).

f: 673. What has already been discussed regarding selling one cloth out of two with an option?
b: The detailed rulings and subsidiary cases of this issue were discussed earlier in the text.

f: 674. What is meant by selling grazing lands (marāʿī) in this chapter?
b: What is intended is pasture (kalāʾ), meaning natural grazing areas.

f: 675. Why is selling pasture (kalāʾ) invalid?
b: Because the seller does not own it. People share rights in pasture according to the prophetic tradition.

f: 676. Why is leasing pasture (kalāʾ) invalid?
b: Because the lease concerns consuming the substance itself, which is something permitted for everyone rather than privately owned property.

f: 677. What analogy is used to show why leasing pasture is invalid?
b: If it is invalid to lease privately owned property merely for consuming its substance, such as leasing a cow only to drink its milk, then leasing public pasture is even more clearly invalid.

f: 678. What is the ruling on selling bees according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: They hold that selling bees is not permissible.

f: 679. What is Muḥammad's position regarding the sale of bees?
b: Muḥammad holds that bees may be sold if they are confined and secured. This is also the opinion of al-Shāfiʿī.

f: 680. What evidence do Muḥammad and al-Shāfiʿī use to permit selling bees?
b: They argue that bees are animals with recognized benefit both legally and practically, so they may be sold even though they are not eaten, just like mules and donkeys.

f: 681. How do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله respond to the argument that bees have benefit?
b: They argue that bees belong to the category of creeping creatures (hawām), whose sale is invalid, like wasps. Their benefit comes from what they produce rather than from the bees themselves.

f: 682. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله not consider bees valuable property before honey is produced?
b: Because the benefit is found in their product (honey), not in the bees themselves. Therefore, the bees are not considered beneficial property independently.

f: 683. If someone sells a beehive containing honey together with the bees, is the sale of the bees valid?
b: Yes, according to al-Karkhī's explanation, because the bees are included as something subordinate to the honey.

f: 684. What is Abū Ḥanīfah's رحمه الله ruling regarding selling silkworms?
b: He holds that selling silkworms is not permissible because they are among creeping creatures.

f: 685. What is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله ruling regarding selling silkworms?
b: He permits selling them after they have produced silk, with the worms included as something subordinate to the silk.

f: 686. What is Muḥammad's ruling regarding selling silkworms?
b: He permits selling them in all cases because they are beneficial property.

f: 687. What is the ruling on selling silkworm eggs according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله does not permit selling silkworm eggs.

f: 688. What is the ruling on selling silkworm eggs according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: They permit selling them due to necessity.

f: 689. Is there another narration regarding Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله position on silkworm eggs?
b: Yes. It is reported that Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله agrees with Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله regarding silkworm eggs, just as he does regarding silkworms.

f: 690. Under what conditions may pigeons be sold?
b: Pigeons may be sold when their number is known and delivery is possible because they are property capable of delivery.

f: 691. What is the ruling on selling a runaway slave (ābiq)?
b: It is not permissible.

f: 692. Why is selling a runaway slave invalid?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ prohibited it and because the seller cannot deliver the slave.

f: 693. When is selling a runaway slave permissible?
b: It is permissible if the buyer claims that the slave is already in his possession.

f: 694. Why is selling a runaway slave to someone who already possesses him permissible?
b: Because the slave is not considered a runaway relative to that purchaser, and the inability to deliver—the reason for prohibition—is absent.

f: 695. Does a purchaser who already possesses a runaway slave become the legal possessor merely through the sale contract?
b: No. Existing possession does not automatically become possession through sale.

f: 696. If a runaway slave was held by the purchaser as a deposit (amānah), does this count as possession for the sale?
b: No. Possession as a trustee does not count as possession under the sale contract.

f: 697. If a runaway slave was held by the purchaser through unlawful seizure (ghaṣb), does this count as possession for the sale?
b: Yes. Possession as a usurper is sufficient, so delivery is already established.

f: 698. What is the ruling on selling a runaway slave (ābiq), and what is the reasoning behind it?
b: It is not permissible to sell a runaway slave because the Prophet ﷺ prohibited it and because delivery is not possible.

f: 699. When is the sale of a runaway slave valid according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: If the buyer claims that the slave is already in his possession, the sale is valid because the slave is not considered a runaway relative to him and the inability to deliver no longer exists.

f: 700. If a person says, "The runaway slave is with so-and-so; sell him to me," and the seller sells him, what is the ruling?
b: The sale is invalid because the slave remains a runaway with respect to both parties and delivery is impossible.

f: 701. If a runaway slave returns after being sold, does the original sale become effective?
b: According to the main view, no, because the sale was originally invalid due to the absence of a valid subject matter, similar to selling a bird in flight.

f: 702. What narration is reported from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله regarding a runaway slave who returns after sale?
b: A narration states that if the contract has not been rescinded, it becomes effective once the slave returns because the slave remained property and only the inability to deliver was removed.

f: 703. What is the ruling on selling a woman's milk in a container?
b: It is not permissible because human body parts are honored and cannot be treated as merchandise.

f: 704. What was al-Shāfiʿī's position regarding selling human milk?
b: He considered it permissible because it is a pure liquid suitable for drinking.

f: 705. Does the prohibition of selling human milk apply to both free women and slave women according to the apparent narration?
b: Yes. There is no distinction between the milk of a free woman and that of a slave woman.

f: 706. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله position regarding the milk of a slave woman?
b: He held that it may be sold because contracts may be made over the person of a slave woman, and therefore over a part of her.

f: 707. Why did the Ḥanafīs reject Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله reasoning regarding slave women's milk?
b: Because slavery affects only the person's ownership, not the milk itself. Ownership applies to living things, whereas milk has no independent life.

f: 708. What is the ruling on selling pig hair?
b: It is not permissible because the pig is intrinsically impure and selling it would amount to honoring something the Sharīʿah commands to be degraded.

f: 709. Why is using pig hair for stitching leather permissible despite the prohibition on selling it?
b: Because necessity requires its use, as certain crafts cannot ordinarily be completed without it.

f: 710. Why does necessity permit using pig hair but not selling it?
b: Because the necessity concerns benefiting from it in a craft, while selling it is unnecessary since other lawful materials can be traded.

f: 711. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله view if pig hair falls into a small amount of water?
b: He held that it makes the water impure.

f: 712. What was Muḥammad's view regarding pig hair falling into water?
b: He held that it does not make the water impure because permission to benefit from it indicates purity.

f: 713. How did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله respond to Muḥammad's argument about pig hair purity?
b: He said that permission is limited to cases of necessity and does not extend to unrelated situations such as contamination of water.

f: 714. What is the ruling on selling human hair or benefiting from it?
b: It is not permissible to sell human hair or benefit from it because the human being is honored and his body parts cannot be treated as objects of commercial exchange or humiliation.

f: 715. Why is selling human hair prohibited according to the jurists?
b: Because human beings are honored in the Sharīʿah, and using their body parts for trade or degrading purposes contradicts that honor.

f: 716. What prophetic narration is used as evidence regarding human hair?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah has cursed the woman who attaches hair extensions and the woman who seeks them."

f: 717. Is there any exception to the prohibition of hair extensions?
b: Yes. Hair made from animal wool, which women use to increase the size of their braids or locks, is permitted.

f: 718. What is the ruling on selling the hides of carrion before tanning?
b: It is not permissible because untanned carrion hides cannot yet be lawfully benefited from.

f: 719. What evidence is mentioned for the prohibition of using untanned carrion hides?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not derive benefit from the hide of a dead animal."

f: 720. What does the term ihāb refer to in the discussion of carrion hides?
b: It refers to an untanned hide, as explained previously in the Book of Prayer.

f: 721. Why is selling and benefiting from carrion hides permissible after tanning?
b: Because tanning purifies the hide and makes it suitable for lawful benefit.

f: 722. What is the ruling on the bones, sinews, wool, horns, hair, and fur of a dead animal?
b: There is no objection to selling or benefiting from them because death does not affect them, as they do not contain life.

f: 723. Why are the bones, horns, wool, and similar parts of a dead animal considered pure?
b: Because they do not possess life, so death does not transfer impurity to them.

f: 724. What was Muḥammad's opinion regarding elephant bones?
b: Muḥammad considered the elephant intrinsically impure like the pig, so its bones would not be treated as pure.

f: 725. What was the opinion of Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله regarding elephants?
b: They regarded elephants like predatory animals, so their bones may be sold and benefited from.

f: 726. What is the ruling if the lower floor of a building belongs to one person and the upper floor belongs to another, and the upper owner sells his upper floor after collapse?
b: The sale is invalid because the right to rebuild upon the lower structure (ḥaqq al-taʿlī) is not considered property.

f: 727. Why is the right to build an upper story (ḥaqq al-taʿlī) not considered property?
b: Because property must be something that can be possessed and controlled, while this right alone cannot independently be possessed in that manner.

f: 728. What is the difference between ḥaqq al-taʿlī and water rights (ḥaqq al-shurb)?
b: A water right represents a share in the water itself, whereas the right to build upward is merely a benefit attached to another property and is not independent property.

f: 729. Can water rights (ḥaqq al-shurb) be sold?
b: Yes. According to all narrations they may be sold together with land, and according to one narration they may even be sold independently.

f: 730. Which scholars preferred the view that water rights may be sold independently?
b: The scholars of Balkh preferred this narration.

f: 731. Why are water rights considered property while the right to build upward is not?
b: Because a water right represents ownership of a portion of the water, and if it is destroyed compensation is due, showing that it has financial value.

f: 732. Why does the destruction of a water right require compensation?
b: Because it is treated as having a share of the purchased value, unlike a mere non-property benefit such as the right to build upward.

f: 733. What is the ruling on selling or gifting a right of way (ṭarīq)?
b: The sale and gift of a right of way are valid.

f: 734. What is the ruling on selling or gifting a watercourse (masīl al-māʾ)?
b: The sale and gift of a watercourse are invalid.

f: 735. What are the two possible interpretations of the ruling regarding the right of way and watercourse?
b: It may refer either to selling the land itself that forms the road or watercourse, or to selling the right of passage or the right to channel water.

f: 736. If the sale of a right of way refers to the land itself, why is it valid?
b: Because the roadway is a known and defined piece of land with a measurable length and width, making it identifiable property.

f: 737. Why is the sale of land forming a watercourse invalid?
b: Because the area occupied by flowing water cannot be precisely determined, making the subject matter uncertain.

f: 738. According to one narration, why is the right of passage valid to sell?
b: Because it is known through its attachment to a specific place, namely the roadway itself.

f: 739. Why is a watercourse running over a roof compared to the right of elevation (ḥaqq al-taʿlī)?
b: Because both relate to uncertain benefits attached to a structure rather than clearly defined property.

f: 740. Why is a watercourse running across the ground considered uncertain?
b: Because the exact place through which the water will flow cannot be determined.

f: 741. According to one narration, what is the difference between the right of passage and the right of elevation?
b: The right of elevation relates to something temporary, namely a building, while the right of passage relates to permanent land.

f: 742. Why is the right of passage treated like tangible property while the right of elevation resembles usufruct?
b: Because land is permanent and independently possessed, whereas a building and its associated benefits may cease to exist.

f: 743. What is the ruling if someone sells something described as a slave-girl but it turns out to be a slave-boy?
b: The sale is invalid and no sale exists between the parties.

f: 744. How does the case of a slave-girl turning out to be a slave-boy differ from selling a ram that turns out to be a ewe?
b: In the case of the ram and ewe, the sale remains valid and the buyer has the option to rescind, whereas in the slave case the sale is void.

f: 745. What principle explains the difference between a slave-girl turning into a slave-boy and a ram turning into a ewe?
