f: 1087. May someone sell a slave-girl by murābaḥah without disclosing that one of her eyes became defective after purchase?
b: Yes, provided the defect occurred without the seller retaining compensation corresponding to part of the purchase price. Physical attributes are incidental to the property and are not separately allocated any portion of the price.

f: 1088. May someone sell a previously married slave-girl by murābaḥah without disclosing that he had intercourse with her?
b: Yes, provided the intercourse did not reduce her market value. The benefit of lawful intercourse is not treated as corresponding to a portion of the purchase price.

f: 1089. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding selling a slave-girl by murābaḥah after one of her eyes became defective?
b: Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله held that the defect must be disclosed before selling by murābaḥah, just as when the seller has retained part of what he originally purchased. Al-Shāfiʿī held the same view.

f: 1090. When must the seller disclose damage to a slave-girl's eye before selling her by murābaḥah?
b: If the seller himself destroyed the eye, or a third party destroyed it and the seller received compensation, he must disclose this because the eye has become an independently compensable part of the property whose value corresponds to part of the purchase price.

f: 1091. Why must loss of virginity be disclosed before selling a slave-girl by murābaḥah?
b: Because virginity is regarded as part of the physical substance of the body that corresponds to part of the purchase price. By removing it, the seller has effectively retained part of the value and must disclose that fact.

f: 1092. May someone sell a garment by murābaḥah without mentioning that it was damaged by mice or fire?
b: Yes. Damage caused by external accidents does not represent a benefit or compensation retained by the seller, so disclosure is not required.

f: 1093. When must damage to a garment be disclosed before selling it by murābaḥah?
b: If the garment became torn through the seller's own repeated unfolding and folding, disclosure is required because the damage resulted from the seller's own use, meaning he effectively retained part of what he originally purchased.

f: 1094. What is the ruling if someone purchases a slave on deferred payment and then sells him by murābaḥah without disclosing the deferment?
b: If the buyer later discovers the concealment, he has the option either to rescind the sale or to accept it.

f: 1095. Why must deferred payment be disclosed in a murābaḥah sale?
b: Because deferment is treated as resembling part of the purchased property, since additional time often justifies a higher price. Murābaḥah is a trust-based sale, so concealing this information violates the buyer's expectation of honesty.

f: 1096. Why is concealment of deferment treated similarly to concealing a defect?
b: Because murābaḥah is founded upon truthful disclosure of all matters affecting the original purchase. Concealing the deferment breaches that trust, so the buyer receives the option to rescind, just as he would upon discovering a defect.

f: 1097. If the buyer destroys or consumes the slave before discovering that the original purchase was deferred, what must he pay in a murābaḥah sale?
b: He remains liable for the full agreed price of one thousand one hundred dirhams because the period of deferment does not correspond to an independent portion of the purchase price.

f: 1098. What is the ruling if an item is transferred by tawliyyah without disclosing that the original purchase was on deferred payment?
b: If the buyer discovers the concealment, he has the option to rescind the sale because tawliyyah, like murābaḥah, is founded upon truthful disclosure of the original purchase price.

f: 1099. If the buyer destroys or consumes an item transferred by tawliyyah before discovering the concealed deferment, what must he pay?
b: He owes the original purchase price of one thousand dirhams payable immediately because the deferred term does not itself correspond to a separate portion of the price.

f: 1100. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله alternate opinion regarding a tawliyyah sale in which deferment was concealed and the item was destroyed?
b: He held that the buyer should return the current value of the item and recover the entire purchase price, drawing an analogy to cases involving acceptance of debased coins in place of higher-quality coins.

f: 1101. What alternative method did some jurists suggest for calculating compensation when deferment was concealed in tawliyyah?
b: They suggested valuing the item once as though sold for cash and once as though sold on deferred payment, with the buyer recovering the difference between the two valuations.

f: 1102. Must customary deferred payment be disclosed in murābaḥah and tawliyyah if it was not expressly stated in the original contract?
b: One opinion says yes, because established commercial custom has the force of an express contractual stipulation. Another opinion says no, because the stated purchase price remains payable immediately in legal terms.

f: 1103. What is the ruling if someone transfers an item at "whatever it cost me" while the buyer does not know the original cost?
b: The sale is invalid because the purchase price is unknown.

f: 1104. What happens if the seller informs the buyer of the original cost during the same contractual session?
b: The buyer may either proceed with the purchase or refuse it. Since the defect is cured before the session ends, the sale is treated as though the price had been known from the outset.

f: 1105. Why can ignorance of the original cost be cured if clarified during the same contractual session?
b: Because the contractual defect has not yet become final. Clarifying the price before the parties separate is treated like delayed acceptance within the same session, allowing the contract to become valid.

f: 1106. Why does the buyer still receive an option after the original cost is disclosed during the same contractual session?
b: Because his initial consent was not fully informed due to ignorance of the price. The option protects that incomplete consent and is analogous to the option granted after inspecting goods (khiyār al-ruʾyah).

f: 1107. May a purchaser sell movable property before taking possession of it?
b: No. A purchaser may not sell movable property before taking possession because the Prophet ﷺ prohibited selling property before possession, and before possession there remains the possibility that the contract will be dissolved if the property perishes.

f: 1108. Why is selling movable property before possession prohibited?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ forbade selling property before possession, and because the contract remains vulnerable to dissolution if the property is destroyed before possession is taken.

f: 1109. May immovable property be sold before possession according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Yes. They held that immovable property may be sold before possession because the essential elements of a valid sale have been completed and the risk of destruction is minimal.

f: 1110. What was Muḥammad's opinion regarding selling immovable property before possession?
b: Muḥammad held that it is not permissible, relying upon the general wording of the prophetic prohibition against selling property before possession and by analogy with movable property.

f: 1111. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله permit selling immovable property before possession?
b: Because the sale has already been completed between competent parties concerning a valid subject matter, and the uncertainty that justifies the prohibition is absent since immovable property is rarely destroyed before possession.

f: 1112. What type of uncertainty does the prophetic prohibition against selling before possession seek to prevent?
b: It seeks to prevent the uncertainty arising from the possible dissolution of the contract if the property is destroyed before possession is taken.

f: 1113. How did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله reconcile the prophetic prohibition with their ruling on immovable property?
b: They interpreted the ḥadīth in light of its underlying reason—the risk of contractual dissolution—which generally exists for movable property but not for immovable property.

f: 1114. How did Muḥammad support his opinion by analogy with leasing (ijārah)?
b: He compared selling immovable property before possession to leasing, arguing that both should follow the same rule.

f: 1115. How did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله answer the analogy with leasing?
b: They noted that even if the same disagreement applies to leasing, the subject matter of a lease is usufruct (manfaʿah), whose destruction is also uncommon, so the rationale for prohibition is weak.

f: 1116. Must a purchaser remeasure or reweigh goods before reselling them by measure or weight?
b: Yes. Whoever buys measured goods by measure or weighed goods by weight must measure or weigh them again before reselling them by measure or weight.

f: 1117. May the second purchaser consume measured or weighed goods before remeasuring or reweighing them?
b: No. The second purchaser may neither sell nor consume them until they have been measured or weighed again.

f: 1118. Why must measured or weighed goods be measured or weighed again before resale?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ prohibited selling food until both the seller and the buyer have measured it, and because the actual quantity may exceed the agreed amount, with any excess belonging to the original seller.

f: 1119. Why does the possibility of excess quantity prevent resale before remeasurement?
b: Because the excess would belong to the original seller, and selling or consuming property that may belong to someone else is unlawful.

f: 1120. Why does this ruling not apply when the goods are resold without measurement (mujāzafah)?
b: Because in a sale without measurement, any excess quantity belongs to the purchaser rather than the original seller.

f: 1121. Why is cloth sold by its measured length treated differently from measured commodities?
b: Because any additional length is merely an attribute of the cloth itself and belongs to the purchaser, whereas additional quantity in measured commodities is treated as separate property belonging to the original seller.

f: 1122. Is the seller's measurement before the sale sufficient to permit the purchaser to resell measured goods?
b: No. Even if the purchaser was present, the seller's measurement before the sale does not suffice because it is not simultaneously the measurement of both seller and purchaser after the sale.

f: 1123. Is the seller's measurement after the sale valid if the purchaser is absent?
b: No. It does not suffice because measurement is part of legal delivery, and valid delivery cannot occur without the purchaser's presence.

f: 1124. Why must the purchaser be present when measured goods are measured after the sale?
b: Because measurement forms part of delivery, and the commodity only becomes fully specified through measurement. Valid delivery requires the purchaser's presence.

f: 1125. If the seller measures the goods after the sale in the purchaser's presence, is a second measurement by the purchaser required?
b: According to some jurists, yes, because the apparent wording of the ḥadīth mentions two measurements. However, the sounder opinion is that a single measurement in the purchaser's presence is sufficient because it completes specification and delivery.

f: 1126. Why is a single measurement after the sale in the purchaser's presence considered sufficient according to the sounder opinion?
b: Because the commodity becomes fully specified through that measurement, genuine delivery takes place, and the purpose of the prophetic instruction is fulfilled.

f: 1127. How is the prophetic requirement of "two measurements" understood according to the sounder opinion?
b: It refers to the involvement of two separate transactions rather than requiring two distinct physical measurements.

f: 1128. How are goods sold by counting treated regarding resale before recounting?
b: According to one narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, they resemble cloth sold by measurement because counting is not a category of ribā goods. According to another narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, they resemble weighed goods because the purchaser is entitled only to the exact number stipulated.

f: 1129. May a purchaser dispose of the purchase price before taking possession of the purchased item?
b: Yes. Disposing of the purchase price before possession is permissible.

f: 1130. Why may the purchase price be disposed of before possession while the purchased item may not?
b: Because ownership of the price already exists without uncertainty arising from possible destruction, and money does not become individually specified through designation in the same way as the purchased commodity.

f: 1131. May the purchaser increase the purchase price in favor of the seller after the contract?
b: Yes. According to the Ḥanafīs, an increase in the price may validly become incorporated into the original contract.

f: 1132. May the seller increase the quantity of the sold item in favor of the purchaser after the contract?
b: Yes. According to the Ḥanafīs, the additional quantity becomes incorporated into the original contract.

f: 1133. May the seller reduce the purchase price after the contract?
b: Yes. According to the Ḥanafīs, a reduction in the price becomes part of the original contract rather than a separate transaction.

f: 1134. How do the Ḥanafīs view increases and reductions made after the sale?
b: They hold that both increases (ziyādah) and reductions (ḥaṭṭ) become incorporated into the original contract, with the legal entitlement attaching to them as though they had originally been part of the agreement.

f: 1135. What was the opinion of Zufar and al-Shāfiʿī regarding increases and reductions after the sale?
b: They held that such increases and reductions do not become attached to the original contract but instead constitute separate gratuitous transfers.

f: 1136. Why did Zufar and al-Shāfiʿī deny that an increase could become part of the original purchase price?
b: Because this would imply that a person acquires ownership of property he already owns in exchange for property he also already owns, which they regarded as legally impossible.

f: 1137. Why did Zufar and al-Shāfiʿī regard a reduction in the purchase price as a separate gift rather than part of the original contract?
b: Because the entire original price already corresponded to the whole of the sold property, leaving nothing that could later be removed from that correspondence. Accordingly, any reduction is simply a new act of charity.

f: 1138. Why do the Ḥanafīs hold that increases and reductions after a sale become part of the original contract?
b: Because the parties are merely changing the contract from one lawful form to another lawful form. Since they have the greater authority to cancel the contract entirely, they also have the lesser authority to modify one of its lawful attributes.

f: 1139. What lawful forms may a sale take after the parties increase or reduce the price?
b: The sale may become profitable (murābaḥah), unprofitable (waḍīʿah), or exactly at cost (tawliyyah).

f: 1140. Why is changing the price after the contract compared to stipulating or waiving an option (khiyār)?
b: Because both involve modifying a lawful attribute of an existing contract rather than creating an entirely new contract.

f: 1141. Why do increases and reductions relate back to the original contract according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because they are attributes of the contract rather than independent transactions. Attributes follow the thing they describe and therefore attach retroactively to the original sale.

f: 1142. Why does complete remission of the entire purchase price not become part of the original contract?
b: Because remitting the entire price changes the substance of the contract itself rather than merely modifying one of its attributes.

f: 1143. How does an increase in the purchase price affect a later murābaḥah or tawliyyah sale?
b: The increase is treated as part of the original cost price and is included when calculating the later murābaḥah or tawliyyah.

f: 1144. How does a reduction in the purchase price affect a later murābaḥah or tawliyyah sale?
b: The reduction is deducted from the original cost price and lowers the basis upon which murābaḥah or tawliyyah is calculated.

f: 1145. How does a valid reduction in the purchase price affect the right of pre-emption (shufʿah)?
b: The pre-emptor acquires the property for the reduced purchase price because the reduction relates back to the original contract.

f: 1146. Is a pre-emptor required to pay a price increase agreed upon after the right of pre-emption has arisen?
b: No. The parties may not defeat the pre-emptor's established right by increasing the price after the right of pre-emption has already come into existence.

f: 1147. Is an increase in the purchase price valid after the sold property has perished?
b: No. According to the apparent narration, an increase is ineffective because the property no longer exists in a state capable of supporting additional consideration.

f: 1148. Why is an increase invalid after the sold property has perished?
b: Because a legal ruling must first have an existing subject to which it can attach. Once the property has perished, there is no remaining subject capable of bearing the increase.

f: 1149. Why is a reduction in the purchase price still valid after the sold property has perished?
b: Because it remains possible to remove part of the consideration corresponding to the sold property even after the property itself has been destroyed.

f: 1150. May a seller who sold on immediate payment later grant the buyer a period of deferment?
b: Yes. The debt becomes deferred because the purchase price is the seller's own right, and he may postpone demanding it.

f: 1151. Why may a seller defer payment after originally stipulating immediate payment?
b: Because he has authority over his own right. Since he could completely forgive the debt, he certainly has the lesser authority to postpone its payment.

f: 1152. What is the ruling if payment is deferred to a highly uncertain time, such as "until the wind blows"?
b: The deferment is invalid because the uncertainty is excessive.

f: 1153. What is the ruling if payment is deferred to a relatively uncertain time, such as "until the harvest" or "until threshing"?
b: The deferment is valid because the uncertainty is slight and is tolerated under the same principles applied in the chapter on guarantees (kafālah).

f: 1154. Does every immediately payable debt become deferred if the creditor grants additional time?
b: Yes. Every immediately payable debt becomes deferred when the creditor grants deferment, except for a loan (qarḍ).

f: 1155. Does deferment become legally binding in the case of a loan (qarḍ)?
b: No. Deferment of a loan is not legally binding according to the Ḥanafīs.

f: 1156. Why is deferment of a loan not legally effective?
b: Because a loan combines two legal aspects: at its inception it is an act of benevolence, while at its conclusion it resembles a commercial exchange. Under either aspect, binding deferment is not legally recognized.

f: 1157. Why is a loan regarded as an act of benevolence at its inception?
b: Because it is intended as assistance rather than commercial gain. For this reason, it may be concluded simply by saying, "I lend it to you," and only someone with authority to make gratuitous transfers may grant it.

f: 1158. Who may not validly grant a loan?
b: A person who lacks authority to make gratuitous transfers, such as a guardian acting beyond his authority or a minor, may not validly grant a loan.

f: 1159. Why is deferment not binding if a loan is viewed as an act of benevolence?
b: Because conditions attached to gratuitous acts of charity are generally not legally enforceable, and charitable acts are not subject to legal compulsion.

f: 1160. Why is deferment also invalid if a loan is viewed as a commercial exchange?
b: Because it would amount to exchanging money for money on a deferred basis, which constitutes ribā.

f: 1161. What is the ruling if someone bequeaths that one thousand dirhams from his estate be loaned to a specific person for one year?
b: The heirs must lend the money from one-third of the estate and may not demand repayment before the year has elapsed.

f: 1162. Why is deferment binding in the case of a testamentary loan?
b: Because the bequest itself is a charitable disposition by the deceased. Fulfilling the specified period honors the testator's charitable intention, similar to bequests granting residence in a house or use of a servant.

f: 1163. How is ribā defined in exchanges of measured or weighed commodities?
b: Ribā is prohibited whenever commodities sold by measure or by weight are exchanged for others of the same kind in unequal quantities.

f: 1164. What is the effective legal cause (ʿillah) of ribā according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: The effective cause is the combination of common genus with either measurement (kayl) or weight (wazn).

f: 1165. What broader formulation of the effective cause of ribā is also mentioned?
b: Some jurists stated that the effective cause is simply quantity together with common genus, treating quantity as the broader underlying concept behind measurement and weight.

f: 1166. What is the foundational ḥadīth regarding ribā in exchanges?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Wheat for wheat, equal for equal, hand to hand; any excess is ribā." He also applied the same ruling to barley, dates, salt, gold, and silver.

f: 1167. Which six commodities are specifically mentioned in the ḥadīth of ribā?
b: Wheat, barley, dates, salt, gold, and silver.

f: 1168. What does the Prophet's ﷺ requirement of "equal for equal" establish?
b: It establishes that when the same ribā commodity is exchanged for itself, the exchange must be equal in quantity and immediate; any excess constitutes ribā.

f: 1169. What are the two grammatical forms in which the ḥadīth is transmitted?
b: The ḥadīth is transmitted as mithlun bi-mithlin ("equal for equal") and mithlan bi-mithlin ("exchange equally" or "sell equal for equal").

f: 1170. What does the wording mithlun bi-mithlin mean?
b: It means that one quantity of wheat is exchanged for an equal quantity of wheat.

f: 1171. What does the wording mithlan bi-mithlin mean?
b: It means that wheat should be exchanged in equal quantities.

f: 1172. On what point do all jurists who accept analogical reasoning agree regarding the ḥadīth of ribā?
b: They agree upon the legal ruling prohibiting unequal exchange of the specified commodities. Their disagreement concerns the underlying effective legal cause (ʿillah).

f: 1173. What is the effective cause (ʿillah) for ribā in foodstuffs according to al-Shāfiʿī?
b: The effective cause is edibility (ṭaʿm).

f: 1174. What is the effective cause (ʿillah) for ribā in gold and silver according to al-Shāfiʿī?
b: The effective cause is their monetary quality (thamaniyyah).

f: 1175. What role does common genus play in al-Shāfiʿī's theory of ribā?
b: Common genus is a condition for the ruling rather than the effective legal cause itself.

f: 1176. Why does al-Shāfiʿī regard equality in exchange as necessary?
b: Because equal exchange is the means by which ribā is avoided when the effective legal cause and common genus are both present.

f: 1177. Why does al-Shāfiʿī regard prohibition as the original rule in these exchanges?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ required both immediate exchange and equality, indicating that these commodities possess exceptional legal significance requiring special regulation.

f: 1178. How does al-Shāfiʿī explain the legal significance of foodstuffs?
b: He argues that food preserves human life, making it a suitable effective cause for the prohibition of ribā.

f: 1179. How does al-Shāfiʿī explain the legal significance of gold and silver?
b: He argues that gold and silver preserve wealth, upon which people's worldly interests depend, making their monetary quality the effective cause of ribā.

f: 1180. Why does al-Shāfiʿī reject common genus as the effective cause of ribā?
b: Because common genus does not itself explain the special legal importance reflected in the ḥadīth. He therefore treats it as a condition rather than the underlying cause.

f: 1181. Can a legal ruling depend upon a condition as well as an effective cause according to al-Shāfiʿī?
b: Yes. Al-Shāfiʿī holds that a legal ruling may revolve around a condition just as it revolves around an effective legal cause.

f: 1182. Why do the Ḥanafīs require equality when exchanging ribā commodities of the same kind?
b: Because the Prophet ﷺ made equality a condition of a valid exchange. Equality preserves the true nature of sale, protects wealth from unjust loss, and perfects the transaction through reciprocal fairness and simultaneous delivery.

f: 1183. What purposes are served by requiring equality in ribā exchanges according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: It realizes the reciprocal nature of sale, protects people's wealth from unjust loss, and perfects the benefit of the transaction by ensuring proper exchange.

f: 1184. Why does ribā arise whenever equality is absent?
b: Because any contractually stipulated surplus in an exchange of ribā commodities without a lawful countervalue constitutes ribā.

f: 1185. Upon what does legal equality between two ribā commodities depend according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: It depends upon both physical quantity and legal identity (common genus).

f: 1186. What role does measurement or weight play in establishing equality?
b: Measurement or weight establishes equality in physical quantity between the exchanged commodities.

f: 1187. What role does common genus play in establishing equality?
b: Common genus establishes legal identity between the exchanged commodities, making any surplus legally recognizable as ribā.

f: 1188. How do the Ḥanafīs define ribā?
b: Ribā is a surplus contractually stipulated for one party in an exchange without any lawful countervalue.

f: 1189. Why are differences in quality ignored when exchanging ribā commodities of the same kind?
b: Because commercial custom does not regard quality differences as creating true legal inequality, recognizing them would hinder commerce, and the Prophet ﷺ stated that superior and inferior qualities are legally equal in such exchanges.

f: 1190. What prophetic statement supports disregarding differences in quality?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Its good quality and its inferior quality are equal."

f: 1191. Why do the Ḥanafīs reject edibility and monetary quality as the effective causes of ribā?
b: Because these are among the greatest human necessities, and the Sharīʿah normally regulates necessities by facilitating their use rather than imposing unnecessary restrictions.

f: 1192. Is exchanging measured or weighed commodities of the same kind in equal quantities valid?
b: Yes. When both commodities are of the same genus and exchanged in equal measured or weighed quantities, the condition of equality is fulfilled and the sale is valid.

f: 1193. Which narrations emphasize the requirement of equality through measurement?
b: Some narrations state "measure for measure" regarding measured commodities and "weight for weight" regarding gold and other weighed commodities.

f: 1194. What is the ruling when measured or weighed ribā commodities of the same kind are exchanged in unequal quantities?
b: The exchange is invalid because ribā has been realized through the unequal surplus.

f: 1195. May superior-quality ribā commodities be exchanged for inferior-quality ones in unequal quantities?
b: No. Differences in quality are legally disregarded, so they may only be exchanged in equal quantities.

f: 1196. Is exchanging one handful for two handfuls, or one apple for two apples, considered ribā?
b: No. Such exchanges are permissible because there is no legally recognized standard of measurement applicable to them, so the legal surplus constituting ribā does not arise.

f: 1197. Why are exchanges of handfuls or individual apples exempt from the rules of ribā?
b: Because the Sharīʿah has not established a legal measuring standard for such quantities, making legal equality impossible to determine.

f: 1198. Why is compensation for handfuls or individual apples based on market value rather than exact equivalents if they are destroyed?
b: Because they are not legally classified as measured or weighed fungible goods, so liability is based on market value rather than replacement by an exact equivalent.

f: 1199. Why does al-Shāfiʿī prohibit exchanging one apple for two apples?
b: Because he considers edibility itself to be the effective cause of ribā, and where equality cannot be established, the exchange is prohibited.

f: 1200. How are quantities smaller than half a ṣāʿ treated?
b: They are treated like handfuls because the Sharīʿah does not prescribe a legal measuring standard below half a ṣāʿ.

f: 1201. May weighed or measured non-food commodities of the same kind, such as iron or gypsum, be exchanged in unequal quantities according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: No. The exchange is invalid because the effective cause—common genus together with measurement or weight—is present.

f: 1202. What is al-Shāfiʿī's ruling on exchanging unequal quantities of measured or weighed non-food commodities of the same kind?
b: He permits such exchanges because neither edibility nor monetary quality, which he regards as the effective causes of ribā, is present.

f: 1203. What is the ruling when both the common genus and the accompanying effective cause of ribā are absent?
b: Both inequality in quantity (faḍl) and deferment (nasī'ah) are permissible because the legal cause of ribā is entirely absent.

f: 1204. Why are inequality and deferment permissible when both characteristics of ribā are absent?
b: Because the complete legal cause that gives rise to the prohibition of ribā does not exist.

f: 1205. What is the basic rule when neither of the causes of ribā is present?
b: The basic rule is permissibility, so the transaction is lawful.

f: 1206. What is the ruling when both the common genus and the accompanying effective cause are present?
b: Both inequality (ribā al-faḍl) and deferment (ribā al-nasī'ah) are prohibited because the complete legal cause of ribā exists.

f: 1207. What is the ruling when only one of the two characteristics of ribā is present?
b: Inequality is permissible, but deferment remains prohibited.

f: 1208. Can commodities sharing only one of the characteristics of ribā be exchanged in unequal quantities?
b: Yes. Unequal quantities are permissible when only one characteristic is present, although deferred exchange remains prohibited.

f: 1209. Can commodities sharing only one of the characteristics of ribā be exchanged on deferred terms?
b: No. Deferment is prohibited even when only one characteristic of ribā is present.

f: 1210. What is an example where only the common genus is present?
b: Exchanging Herāt cloth for Herāt cloth, where the commodities share a common genus but lack the accompanying effective cause of measurement or weight.

f: 1211. What is an example where only the accompanying effective cause is present?
b: Exchanging wheat for barley, since both are measured commodities but belong to different genera.

f: 1212. What conditions are required for ribā al-faḍl (usury of excess) according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Ribā al-faḍl requires both the common genus and the accompanying effective cause (measurement or weight).

f: 1213. What conditions are required for ribā al-nasī'ah (usury of deferment) according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Ribā al-nasī'ah requires only one of the two characteristics: either common genus or the accompanying effective cause.

f: 1214. Does al-Shāfiʿī consider common genus by itself sufficient to prohibit deferment?
b: No. Al-Shāfiʿī holds that common genus alone does not prohibit deferment.

f: 1215. Why does al-Shāfiʿī reject common genus alone as a basis for prohibiting deferment?
b: Because common genus merely creates the possibility of excess, and since actual excess is not prohibited in every exchange, a mere possibility of excess deserves prohibition even less.

f: 1216. How do the Ḥanafīs justify prohibiting deferment when only one characteristic of ribā exists?
b: They argue that the property is considered ribā-property from one perspective—either through common measurement or weight, or through common genus—so the legal resemblance to ribā is sufficient to prohibit deferment.

f: 1217. How does monetary quality contribute to the Ḥanafī reasoning regarding ribā?
b: Monetary quality creates superiority in financial value, giving rise to the possibility of ribā. This legal resemblance is sufficient to justify prohibition, even if actual ribā has not yet occurred.

f: 1218. Why do the Ḥanafīs treat the possibility of ribā as legally significant?
b: Because a legal resemblance to ribā is sufficient to justify prohibition, just as actual ribā itself would prohibit the transaction.

f: 1219. Is there an exception to the general ribā rules for weighed commodities?
b: Yes. Advancing money through a salam contract in exchange for saffron and similar commodities is permissible even though both are sold by weight.

f: 1220. Why is salam with money for saffron permitted despite both being weighed?
b: Because the nature of their weight differs fundamentally. Coins function as currency, while saffron is merchandise, so they are not legally equivalent despite both being weighed.

f: 1221. How is saffron weighed?
b: Saffron is weighed using merchants' scales.

f: 1222. How are coins weighed?
b: Coins are weighed using mint weights.

f: 1223. What is the legal status of saffron in commercial transactions?
b: Saffron is merchandise (muthman) and becomes specifically identified by designation.

f: 1224. What is the legal status of coins in commercial transactions?
b: Coins function as currency (thaman) and do not become specifically identified merely by designation.

f: 1225. May someone dispose of weighed coins after taking possession of them without weighing them again?
b: Yes. Once the purchaser has taken possession of weighed coins, he may dispose of them before weighing them again.

f: 1226. Does the same ruling apply to saffron and similar commodities?
b: No. Saffron and similar goods may not be disposed of before being properly weighed.

f: 1227. In what ways do coins and saffron differ according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: They differ in appearance, legal meaning, and legal rulings.

f: 1228. Why does the shared characteristic of weight not create ribā between coins and saffron?
b: Because their differences prevent weight from being a complete common characteristic. The resemblance to ribā becomes too weak to have legal effect.

f: 1229. What degree of resemblance to ribā has no legal effect according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: A mere "resemblance of a resemblance" (shubhat al-shubhah) carries no legal effect.

f: 1230. What is the ruling regarding commodities explicitly mentioned by the Prophet ﷺ as measured commodities?
b: They remain legally measured commodities forever, even if people later abandon measuring them in commercial practice.

f: 1231. Which commodities permanently retain the legal ruling of being measured?
b: Wheat, barley, dates, and salt remain legally measured commodities because the Prophet ﷺ explicitly treated them as such.

f: 1232. What is the ruling regarding commodities explicitly mentioned by the Prophet ﷺ as weighed commodities?
b: They remain legally weighed commodities forever, even if commercial custom later changes.

f: 1233. Which commodities permanently retain the legal ruling of being weighed?
b: Gold and silver remain legally weighed commodities because the Prophet ﷺ explicitly treated them as such.

f: 1234. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad maintain the original standards of measurement and weight despite changes in custom?
b: Because revealed texts are stronger than commercial custom, and a stronger proof is not displaced by a weaker one.

f: 1235. How are commodities not specifically mentioned in the prophetic texts classified?
b: They are classified according to the prevailing custom of the people because custom serves as a legal indicator.

f: 1236. What is Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله opinion regarding commodities explicitly mentioned in the texts?
b: He holds that even those commodities should follow prevailing commercial custom.

f: 1237. Why does Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله believe the legal standard should follow changing custom?
b: Because he considers the Prophet's ﷺ reference to measurement or weight to have reflected the custom of his time. When custom changes, the legal application should also change.

f: 1238. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, is exchanging wheat for wheat by equal weight valid if wheat is customarily sold by weight?
b: No. It remains invalid because wheat is legally classified as a measured commodity regardless of commercial custom.

f: 1239. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad, is exchanging gold for gold by equal volume valid if custom changes?
b: No. Gold remains legally a weighed commodity, so exchanging it by equal measure rather than equal weight is invalid.

f: 1240. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad reject exchanges based on changed commercial standards?
b: Because inequality remains possible according to the legally recognized standard established by the revealed texts.

f: 1241. To what do the Ḥanafīs compare exchanging commodities according to an unrecognized standard?
b: They compare it to selling goods without measurement (mujāzafah), where the true quantity remains uncertain.

f: 1242. Is salam in wheat by weight valid according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Yes. Salam by weight is valid because the purpose of salam is merely to specify the commodity sufficiently, not to determine the ribā standard governing spot exchanges.

f: 1243. How is anything sold by the pound (raṭl) legally classified?
b: Anything sold according to the pound (raṭl), or another unit derived from weight such as the ūqiyyah, is legally classified as a weighed commodity.

f: 1244. Does the same ruling apply to ordinary measuring vessels?
b: No. Ordinary measuring vessels are treated differently from units derived from weight.

f: 1245. What is the ruling if a weighed commodity is exchanged using unknown measuring containers?
b: The transaction is invalid because the actual weights may differ, creating the possibility of inequality.

f: 1246. Why is exchanging weighed goods using unknown measuring containers invalid?
b: Because the actual weight remains uncertain, making unequal exchange possible. This resembles selling without proper measurement.

f: 1247. What is ṣarf?
b: Ṣarf is a contract involving the exchange of monetary commodities, such as gold for silver or one currency for another.

f: 1248. What condition must be fulfilled for a valid contract of ṣarf?
b: Both counter-values must be taken into possession during the same contractual session.

f: 1249. What prophetic evidence establishes the requirement of possession in ṣarf?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Silver for silver: hā' wa hā'"—that is, "hand to hand."

f: 1250. Does simultaneous possession apply to all ribā commodities?
b: No. Simultaneous possession is specifically required for ṣarf. Other ribā commodities require specific identification but not possession during the same session.

f: 1251. What is required for ribā commodities other than currency according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: They must be specifically identified, but they do not have to be exchanged through simultaneous possession during the same session.

f: 1252. What is al-Shāfiʿī's opinion regarding food commodities?
b: Al-Shāfiʿī requires immediate possession for food commodities as well, based on the prophetic instruction "hand to hand."

f: 1253. Why does al-Shāfiʿī require immediate possession for food?
b: He argues that delaying possession creates successive delivery, and immediate payment possesses legal superiority, giving rise to a resemblance to ribā.

f: 1254. Why do the Ḥanafīs not require immediate possession for non-currency ribā commodities?
b: Because such commodities are individually identified goods, and once identified, the purpose of the sale is achieved without requiring immediate delivery.

f: 1255. What is the purpose of a sale according to the Ḥanafīs in this context?
b: The purpose is to enable lawful ownership and disposal of specifically identified property.

f: 1256. Why does ṣarf differ from the sale of ordinary goods?
b: Because possession itself is what legally identifies the exchanged currencies, making immediate possession an essential requirement.

f: 1257. How do the Ḥanafīs interpret the Prophet's ﷺ statement "hand to hand" regarding non-currency ribā commodities?
b: They interpret it as meaning "specific item for specific item," emphasizing identification rather than immediate physical possession.

f: 1258. Which Companion narrated the wording supporting the Ḥanafī interpretation?
b: ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated the wording supporting this interpretation.

f: 1259. Why do the Ḥanafīs reject the argument that successive possession creates ribā?
b: Because commercial custom does not regard successive possession as creating financial inequality. The significant distinction is between immediate payment and deferred payment, not between simultaneous and successive delivery within the contract.

f: 1260. Is it permissible to exchange one egg for two eggs?
b: Yes. Eggs have no legally recognized measuring standard, so ribā does not arise.

f: 1261. Is it permissible to exchange one date for two dates?
b: Yes, provided the dates are not commodities governed by legal measurement in this context as individual pieces. Individual dates have no legally recognized measuring standard, so ribā does not arise.

f: 1262. Is it permissible to exchange one walnut for two walnuts?
b: Yes. Walnuts have no legally recognized measuring standard, so exchanging them unequally is permissible.

f: 1263. Why are unequal exchanges of eggs, dates, and walnuts permissible according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Because these individual items are not sold according to a legally recognized standard of measure or weight, so the effective cause of ribā is absent.

f: 1264. Why does al-Shāfiʿī prohibit exchanging one egg, date, or walnut for two?
b: Because he considers edibility itself to be the effective cause of ribā, regardless of whether the items are sold by measure or weight.

f: 1265. May one specified copper coin (fals) be exchanged for two specified copper coins according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Yes. Such an exchange is permissible because the designated coins are treated as specifically identified property rather than currency.

f: 1266. What is Muḥammad's ruling on exchanging one specified copper coin for two specified copper coins?
b: He considers it impermissible because copper coins retain their monetary character through public convention and therefore remain subject to the rules of ribā.

f: 1267. Why does Muḥammad prohibit exchanging one specified copper coin for two specified copper coins?
b: Because the monetary nature of copper currency is established by public convention, not merely by the agreement of the contracting parties. Designating particular coins does not remove that monetary status.

f: 1268. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله permit exchanging specified copper coins unequally?
b: Because they hold that monetary status exists between the contracting parties only by their mutual agreement. They may therefore remove that status by agreement, after which the coins become ordinary identified property.

f: 1269. After losing their monetary status, do specified copper coins become weighed commodities?
b: No. They remain counted items because public custom treats them as such.

f: 1270. To what do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله compare exchanging specified copper coins?
b: They compare it to exchanging one walnut for two walnuts, where ribā does not arise.

f: 1271. Why is this ruling different from gold and silver?
b: Because the monetary character of gold and silver is intrinsic and cannot be removed by the agreement of the contracting parties.

f: 1272. Why is exchanging unspecified copper coins not permissible?
b: Because it amounts to exchanging one deferred debt for another, which is invalid.

f: 1273. Why is exchanging one specified copper coin for one unspecified copper coin not permissible?
b: Because common genus alone is sufficient to prohibit deferment in ribā transactions.

f: 1274. Is it permissible to exchange wheat for flour?
b: No. The exchange is not permissible.

f: 1275. Is it permissible to exchange wheat for roasted flour (sawīq)?
b: No. The exchange is not permissible.

f: 1276. Why are wheat, flour, and roasted flour treated as belonging to the same genus?
b: Because flour and roasted flour are merely transformed forms of wheat rather than different commodities.

f: 1277. Why does exchanging wheat for flour remain invalid even if both are measured equally?
b: Because flour and roasted flour are denser than wheat kernels, whose volume includes empty spaces. Equal measures therefore do not represent true equality.

f: 1278. Why does the measuring standard fail to establish equality between wheat and flour?
b: Because the same volume of flour contains more actual substance than the same volume of wheat, making genuine equality impossible despite equal measurement.

f: 1279. May flour be exchanged for flour?
b: Yes. Flour may be exchanged for flour in equal measures because legal equality is achieved.

f: 1280. Why is exchanging flour for flour permissible?
b: Because both commodities are of the same type and equal measurement establishes the required equality.

f: 1281. May flour be exchanged for roasted flour (sawīq) according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: No. Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله holds that exchanging flour for sawīq is invalid whether the quantities are equal or unequal.

f: 1282. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله prohibit exchanging flour for sawīq?
b: Because flour cannot validly be exchanged for roasted grain, nor sawīq for wheat. Since each derivative cannot be exchanged with the other's source, exchanging the derivatives themselves is likewise impermissible.

f: 1283. What is the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding exchanging flour for sawīq?
b: They permit it because they regard flour and sawīq as different genera due to their differing intended uses.

f: 1284. Why do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad consider flour and sawīq to be different genera?
b: Because they focus on the different purposes for which each is used.

f: 1285. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله respond to the argument that flour and sawīq have different uses?
b: He replies that both share the same primary purpose—providing nourishment—and that minor differences in use are legally disregarded.

f: 1286. Is it permissible to exchange meat for a live animal according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله?
b: Yes. They consider such an exchange permissible.

f: 1287. What is Muḥammad's ruling on exchanging meat for a live animal of the same species?
b: He considers it impermissible unless the separated meat exceeds the amount of meat contained within the live animal.

f: 1288. Why does Muḥammad require the exchanged meat to exceed the meat contained in the live animal?
b: So that the meat corresponds to the meat, while the excess corresponds to the animal's remaining parts, thereby avoiding ribā.

f: 1289. According to Muḥammad, what would happen if the exchanged meat did not exceed the meat contained in the live animal?
b: Ribā would arise either through excess meat or through the additional non-meat components of the animal.

f: 1290. To what does Muḥammad compare exchanging meat for a live animal?
b: He compares it to exchanging sesame oil for sesame seeds.

f: 1291. Why do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله permit exchanging meat for a live animal?
b: Because meat is sold by weight, whereas live animals are not ordinarily sold by weight and their weight cannot be accurately determined. Therefore, they are not governed by the same legal measuring standard.

f: 1292. Why are live animals not treated as weighed commodities?
b: Because they are not ordinarily sold by weight and their constantly changing posture prevents accurate weighing.

f: 1293. Is it permissible to exchange fresh dates (ruṭab) for dried dates (tamr) in equal quantities according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Yes. Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله permits exchanging fresh dates for dried dates in equal quantities.

f: 1294. What is the opinion of Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad regarding exchanging fresh dates for dried dates?
b: They prohibit the exchange based on the ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ asked whether fresh dates decrease when they dry and then forbade the exchange.

f: 1295. Which prophetic ḥadīth do Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad rely upon regarding fresh and dried dates?
b: They rely on the ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ asked, "Does it decrease when it dries?" When told yes, he replied, "Then no."

f: 1296. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله argue that fresh dates may be exchanged for dried dates?
b: He argues that fresh dates are still legally called "dates," so the general ḥadīths permitting equal exchanges of dates apply.

f: 1297. What evidence does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله cite to show that fresh dates are still considered "dates"?
b: He cites the narration in which the Prophet ﷺ, when presented with fresh dates from Khaybar, asked, "Are all the dates of Khaybar like this?" referring to fresh dates simply as "dates."

f: 1298. If fresh dates are considered a different type from dried dates, what evidence does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله rely upon?
b: He relies on the Prophet's ﷺ statement, "When the two types differ, sell however you wish."

f: 1299. How does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله critique the ḥadīth prohibiting the exchange of fresh and dried dates?
b: He notes that its chain revolves around Zayd ibn ʿAyyāsh, whom many ḥadīth critics regarded as weak.

f: 1300. Does the disagreement over exchanging fresh dates (ruṭab) for dried dates (tamr) also apply to fresh grapes and raisins?
b: Yes. The same disagreement applies to exchanging fresh grapes for raisins. Some scholars, however, claimed there is consensus prohibiting it by analogy with roasted and unroasted wheat.

f: 1301. According to the Ḥanafīs, may fresh dates be exchanged for fresh dates in equal quantities?
b: Yes. Fresh dates may be exchanged for fresh dates in equal measures because they are still legally regarded as dates.

f: 1302. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, which fresh or moist forms of the same commodity may be exchanged equally?
b: They permit equal exchanges of: (1) fresh dates for fresh dates, (2) moist wheat for moist wheat, (3) moist wheat for dry wheat, (4) soaked dates for soaked dates, and (5) soaked raisins for soaked raisins.

f: 1303. Why does Muḥammad prohibit exchanging moist wheat, dry wheat, soaked dates, and soaked raisins even in equal quantities?
b: Because equality should be judged according to the commodities' most stable (final) state rather than their temporary present condition.

f: 1304. How do Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad differ in determining equality for fresh or moist commodities?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله judges equality according to the commodities' present condition at the time of the exchange, whereas Muḥammad judges it according to their most stable state after drying or settling.

f: 1305. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله distinguish exchanging fresh dates for fresh dates from exchanging fresh dates for dried dates?
b: When fresh dates are exchanged for fresh dates, any future inequality only appears after both items have ceased to be fresh. By contrast, when fresh dates are exchanged for dried dates, one commodity remains fresh while the other is already dried, so the resulting inequality affects the very subject matter of the contract.

f: 1306. May unripe dates (busr) be exchanged for dried dates in unequal quantities?
b: No. Unripe dates are still legally regarded as dates, so unequal exchange is not permitted.

f: 1307. Why may kufrā fruit be exchanged for dates in any ratio while unripe dates (busr) may not?
b: Because kufrā is not legally called "dates" until it fully develops, whereas busr is already legally regarded as dates. Therefore, kufrā is treated as a different commodity.

f: 1308. Why is selling dates for kufrā on deferred payment invalid?
b: Because kufrā is sold by counting, its individual pieces vary considerably, and deferred payment introduces excessive uncertainty (jahālah).

f: 1309. Under what condition may olives be exchanged for olive oil, or sesame seeds for sesame oil?
b: The exchange is only permissible if the amount of oil being exchanged exceeds the amount of oil naturally contained in the olives or sesame seeds. The oil corresponds to the oil naturally contained in the original commodity, while the excess oil corresponds to the remaining solid residue.

f: 1310. Why is exchanging olives for olive oil (or sesame seeds for sesame oil) invalid when the oil is equal to or less than the oil naturally contained in the original commodity?
b: Because the remaining solid residue—or part of the oil together with the residue—would constitute an unlawful surplus, resulting in ribā.

f: 1311. What is the ruling if the amount of oil naturally contained in olives or sesame seeds is unknown?
b: The exchange is impermissible because the possibility of ribā remains, and this possibility is treated as legally equivalent to certainty.

f: 1312. Which other commodity pairs follow the same ruling as olives and olive oil?
b: The same principle applies to: walnuts and walnut oil, milk and clarified butter, grapes and grape juice, and dates and molasses.

f: 1313. What is the ruling on exchanging cotton for spun thread and cloth for raw cotton?
b: The jurists differed regarding exchanging cotton for spun thread. However, they unanimously agreed that cloth may be exchanged for raw cotton in any proportion.

f: 1314. Which types of meat are considered different genera and may therefore be exchanged in unequal quantities?
b: Meat from camels, cattle, and sheep are considered different genera, so they may be exchanged in unequal quantities.

f: 1315. Which animals are treated as the same genus for the purposes of ribā?
b: Cows and buffaloes are one genus; goats and sheep are one genus; Arabian camels and Bactrian camels are one genus.

f: 1316. Why are the meats of camels, cattle, and sheep treated as different genera?
b: Because the original animals are different species. This is reflected in rulings such as zakāh, where the quota of one species cannot be completed by combining it with another.

f: 1317. Are the milks of cows and sheep considered different genera?
b: Yes. According to the Ḥanafīs, cow's milk and sheep's milk are different genera because their original animals are different species, so long as manufacture has not transformed them.

f: 1318. Why does al-Shāfiʿī disagree regarding cow's milk and sheep's milk?
b: He considers them one genus because their intended benefit is the same.

f: 1319. Are grape vinegar and date vinegar considered the same genus?
b: No. They are different genera because their original substances differ. The same principle applies to grape juice and date juice.

f: 1320. Are goat hair and sheep wool considered the same genus?
b: No. They are different genera because their uses differ.

f: 1321. Are abdominal fat, tail fat, and meat considered one genus?
b: No. They are different genera because they differ substantially in their appearance, nature, and utility.

f: 1322. May bread be exchanged for wheat or flour in unequal quantities?
b: Yes. Bread may be exchanged for wheat or flour in unequal quantities because bread is treated as a counted or weighed commodity, whereas wheat remains a measured commodity.

f: 1323. Why may bread be exchanged for wheat or flour in unequal quantities?
b: Because bread is no longer legally classified as a measured commodity in every respect, while wheat remains a measured commodity. Therefore, the effective cause of ribā is not fully shared.

f: 1324. What is the relied-upon (fatwā) position regarding exchanging bread for wheat or flour?
b: The relied-upon position follows the narration permitting the exchange, although another narration from Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله considered it disliked.

f: 1325. What are the rulings on deferred exchange involving bread and wheat?
b: If the wheat is deferred, the exchange remains permissible. If the bread is deferred, Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله also permits it, and this is the relied-upon fatwā.

f: 1326. Is a salam contract in bread valid?
b: Yes. According to the sound opinion, salam in bread is valid.

f: 1327. How did the three Ḥanafī Imāms differ regarding borrowing bread?
b: Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله: disliked borrowing bread by either count or weight because loaves vary. Muḥammad: permitted borrowing by both methods due to widespread commercial practice. Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله: permitted borrowing by weight but not by count because individual loaves differ.

f: 1328. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله dislike borrowing bread?
b: Because loaves vary depending on the baker, the oven, the baking process, and their freshness, making them insufficiently uniform.

f: 1329. When is there no ribā between a master and his slave?
b: There is no ribā between a master and his slave when the slave is authorized to trade and has no outstanding debts, because the slave and all the property in his possession legally belong to the master.

f: 1330. Why can ribā not arise between a master and his debt-free slave?
b: Because the slave and everything in his possession belong to the master, so the transaction is effectively between one person and his own property.

f: 1331. Does ribā apply between a master and a slave who owes debts?
b: Yes. If the slave has debts, ribā may arise between them.

f: 1332. Why may ribā arise between a master and his indebted slave?
b: Because the property in the slave's possession is no longer regarded as belonging exclusively to the master. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, ownership is no longer complete; according to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad, the creditors have acquired rights over the property. Therefore, the slave resembles an unrelated person.

f: 1333. Is ribā possible between a master and his mukātab slave?
b: Yes. Ribā may occur between a master and his mukātab slave because the slave has an independent financial status.

f: 1334. According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله, is there ribā between a Muslim and a belligerent non-Muslim (ḥarbī) in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: No. Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله holds that there is no ribā between a Muslim and a belligerent non-Muslim in Dār al-Ḥarb.

f: 1335. Which jurists disagreed with Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله regarding ribā between a Muslim and a belligerent non-Muslim in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and al-Shāfiʿī disagreed and did not recognize this exception.

f: 1336. What evidence does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله cite for the absence of ribā between a Muslim and a belligerent non-Muslim in Dār al-Ḥarb?
b: He cites the ḥadīth: "There is no ribā between a Muslim and a belligerent non-Muslim in Dār al-Ḥarb." He also argues that the property of belligerent non-Muslims is legally subject to acquisition in their territory, provided no treachery is involved.

f: 1337. Why is a belligerent non-Muslim in Dār al-Ḥarb different from a non-Muslim who enters Muslim lands under safe-conduct (amān)?
b: A non-Muslim under safe-conduct has inviolable property by virtue of the covenant (amān), whereas the property of a belligerent non-Muslim in Dār al-Ḥarb does not enjoy that protection.

f: 1338. When purchasing a residence (manzil) that has another residence above it, when is the upper story included in the sale?
b: The upper story is included only if the buyer purchases the property "with all of its rights," "with its appurtenances," or with wording such as "with everything, great and small, belonging to it or forming part of it."

f: 1339. If someone purchases a room (bayt) and says "with all of its rights," is an upper room automatically included?
b: No. Purchasing a room "with all of its rights" does not include an upper room.

f: 1340. If someone purchases a house (dār) "within its boundaries," what is included?
b: The upper story and the privy are included in the sale because they fall within the boundaries of the house.

f: 1341. What is the legal difference between a dār, bayt, and manzil in sales?
b: Dār (house/compound) includes the entire enclosed property and its integral parts. Bayt (room) refers to a single room, so another room above it is not included. Manzil (dwelling) is intermediate between a dār and a bayt: it resembles a dār enough that the upper story is included when accompanying rights are mentioned, but resembles a bayt enough that it is not included without such wording.

f: 1342. Why is the upper story automatically included when purchasing a dār?
b: Because a dār encompasses everything within its boundaries, and the upper story is one of its integral components and appurtenances.

f: 1343. Why is the upper room not included when purchasing a bayt?
b: Because a bayt refers to a single room, and the upper room is itself another bayt. One thing of the same kind is not treated as an appurtenance of another unless expressly mentioned.

f: 1344. When is the upper story included in the sale of a manzil?
b: It is included when the sale states that it is sold "with all of its rights," "with its appurtenances," or "with everything, great and small." Without such wording, it is not included.

f: 1345. How did some later scholars apply these rulings according to the custom of their own lands?
b: They held that the upper story would be included under all these expressions because, in their custom, every dwelling (khānah) normally included an upper floor.

f: 1346. Is a privy (kanīf) included when purchasing a dār?
b: Yes. A privy is one of the ordinary appurtenances of a dār and is included automatically.

f: 1347. Does a projecting balcony or overhanging structure (ẓullah) automatically pass with the sale of a dār?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله: No. It is included only if the sale uses phrases such as "with all of its rights" or "with its appurtenances." According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله and Muḥammad: Yes, if its entrance opens from inside the house, because it functions as one of the house's appurtenances.

f: 1348. When purchasing a room, dwelling, or residence, is the right of passage automatically included?
b: No. The right of passage is included only if the property is purchased "with all of its rights," "with its appurtenances," or "with everything, great and small."

f: 1349. Are water rights and drainage rights automatically included in the sale of a room, dwelling, or residence?
b: No. Like the right of passage, they are included only when accompanying rights are expressly included in the sale.

f: 1350. Why are passage, water, and drainage rights not automatically included in a sale?
b: Because they lie outside the physical boundaries of the property. They are legal appurtenances rather than physical components, so they pass only when expressly included.

f: 1351. Why is the right of passage automatically included in a lease (ijārah) but not in a sale?
b: In a lease, the purpose is to benefit from the property, and that benefit cannot ordinarily be realized without access. In a sale, ownership itself can still be beneficial without passage rights (for example, by later reselling the property), so those rights are not automatically included.

f: 1352. If someone purchases a slave-girl, she gives birth while in his possession, and another person later proves ownership by legal evidence (bayyinah), who owns the mother and child?
b: The true owner takes both the slave-girl and her child.

f: 1353. If a purchaser merely acknowledges (iqrār) that a slave-girl belongs to another person after she has given birth, does the child also belong to the acknowledged owner?
b: No. The acknowledgment transfers the mother, but the child remains with the purchaser.

f: 1354. Why does a child follow the mother when ownership is established by bayyinah but not by iqrār?
b: Bayyinah is a complete proof that establishes the true owner's ownership retroactively from the outset. Since the child was physically connected to the mother during gestation, it belongs to the true owner. Iqrār is only a limited proof, establishing ownership only to the extent necessary for the acknowledgment, which occurs after the child has become a separate individual.

f: 1355. What is the difference between bayyinah and iqrār regarding retroactive ownership?
b: Bayyinah establishes ownership retroactively from the beginning, whereas iqrār establishes ownership only to the extent necessary for the acknowledgment and not retroactively.

f: 1356. According to the preferred view, is a separate judicial ruling required for the child when ownership of the mother is established?
b: Yes. The preferred view is that the judge must issue a separate ruling concerning the child.

f: 1357. What legal reasoning supports requiring a separate judgment for the child?
b: Muḥammad states that additions or increments to property are not included in a judgment unless the judge is aware of them. Likewise, if the child is in someone else's possession, it is not automatically included in the judgment concerning the mother.

f: 1358. If someone buys a person who later proves to be free, after that person had told the buyer, "Buy me, for I am his slave," and the seller is available, who bears the loss?
b: The purchaser seeks recovery from the seller, and the supposedly enslaved person owes nothing.

f: 1359. If someone buys a person who later proves to be free after that person claimed to be a slave, and the seller's whereabouts are unknown, who is liable?
b: The purchaser recovers from the formerly supposed slave, who then has recourse against the seller.

f: 1360. Why does Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله allow the purchaser to recover from the free person when the seller cannot be found?
b: Because by telling the purchaser, "Buy me, for I am his slave," the person induced the purchase. Since a person's own statement about his freedom or slavery is legally relied upon, this instruction is treated as an implied guarantee protecting the purchaser if recovery from the seller becomes impossible.

f: 1361. Does a person who falsely claimed to be a slave become an implied guarantor according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Muḥammad?
b: Yes. If the purchaser cannot recover from the seller, the person who induced the purchase is treated as having guaranteed the purchase price.

f: 1362. According to Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, can the purchaser recover from the free person who falsely claimed to be a slave?
b: No. Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله holds that there is no recourse because liability arises only from contracts of exchange or guarantees, not from a false statement alone.

f: 1363. If someone accepts as collateral (rahn) a person who claimed to be a slave but is later discovered to be free, does the creditor have recourse against him?
b: No. There is no recourse under any circumstances.

f: 1364. Why is there no recourse in the collateral (rahn) case?
b: Because merely accepting someone as collateral does not involve the kind of reliance that creates an implied guarantee. The person's false statement alone does not establish financial liability.

f: 1365. When is the purchaser allowed to recover from the person who falsely claimed to be a slave according to the Ḥanafīs?
b: Only when recovery from the seller has become impossible because the seller's whereabouts cannot be determined.

f: 1366. Why can someone who induces another to enter a sale be treated as an implied guarantor?
b: Because a sale is a contract of exchange, and by inducing another to enter it, the person is treated as guaranteeing the validity of the exchange if recovery from the seller later becomes impossible.

f: 1367. Why does this implied guarantee not apply to a pledge (rahn)?
b: Because a pledge is not a contract of exchange. It merely serves as security for an existing debt, so directing someone to accept a pledge does not amount to guaranteeing its validity.

f: 1368. What evidence shows that a pledge (rahn) is not treated as a contract of exchange?
b: A pledge may secure obligations arising from ṣarf (currency exchange) or salam, even though substitution is impermissible in those contracts, showing that a pledge merely secures a debt rather than constituting an exchange.

f: 1369. Why does the false statement of an unrelated stranger not create financial liability?
b: Because people do not ordinarily rely on a stranger's statement when entering a transaction, so the legal element of deception that creates implied liability is absent.

f: 1370. If a master says, "Trade with this slave of mine, for I have authorized him," and it later turns out the slave had no authority, who bears the loss?
b: The parties who dealt with the slave recover the value of their loss from the master because he induced them to rely on the slave's supposed authority.

f: 1371. Why is there a difficulty in this discussion according to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله?
b: Because Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله normally requires a slave to assert his claim to freedom, yet the slave had previously stated that he was a slave, and contradictory statements normally invalidate a claim.

f: 1372. How do the jurists explain why the slave's prior admission of slavery does not always bar his later claim to freedom?
b: They offered three explanations: (1) if the issue concerns original free status, no formal claim is required because protecting his freedom also protects his mother's marriage; (2) contradiction is overlooked because the circumstances of conception are inherently hidden; (3) if he claims prior emancipation, contradiction does not matter because emancipation depends solely on the master's declaration.

f: 1373. Give examples where a prior contradictory statement does not invalidate a later legal claim.
b: Examples include: (1) a woman who accepted khulʿ but later proves her husband had already issued three divorces before the khulʿ, and (2) a mukātab who later proves his master had already emancipated him before the manumission contract.

f: 1374. If someone claims only an unspecified right in a house, settles for compensation, and it is later proven that almost the entire house belongs to someone else, may he recover part of the settlement?
b: No. He cannot recover any part of the settlement.

f: 1375. Why can't a claimant recover part of a settlement after a superior claim removes most of the property when he originally claimed only an unspecified right?
b: Because his original claim was unspecified, it remains possible that his claim related to the small portion that remains. Since that possibility still exists, the settlement cannot be partially undone.

f: 1376. If someone claimed ownership of an entire house, settled the claim, and part of the house is later recovered by its true owner, what happens to the settlement?
b: The claimant recovers a proportionate part of the settlement because the portion of the property for which he relinquished his claim did not belong to the defendant.

f: 1377. Why does a claimant recover a proportionate part of the settlement when part of the property is later established to belong to someone else?
b: Because the settlement was made in exchange for relinquishing the claim to the entire property. When part of that subject matter fails, the corresponding portion of the consideration must be returned.

f: 1378. What legal principle regarding settlements does this case establish?
b: A settlement in which an unknown claim is relinquished in exchange for a known amount is valid.

f: 1379. Why is a settlement over an unknown claim valid?
b: Because the uncertainty concerns what is being relinquished, not what is being received, and such uncertainty does not ordinarily lead to disputes.

f: 1380. According to the Ḥanafīs, what is the ruling on a sale made by an unauthorized person (bayʿ al-fuḍūlī)?
b: The sale is suspended (mawqūf): the owner may either ratify it, making it effective, or reject it, causing it to fail.

f: 1381. What is al-Shāfiʿī's ruling on the sale of an unauthorized agent (bayʿ al-fuḍūlī)?
b: It is void from the outset because the seller lacks legal authority to conclude the sale.

f: 1382. According to al-Shāfiʿī, what are the only two sources of legal authority to sell property?
b: Ownership of the property or authorization from its owner.

f: 1383. Why do the Ḥanafīs regard the sale of an unauthorized agent as capable of later ratification?
b: Because it is a transfer of ownership performed by a legally competent person regarding a suitable subject matter, so the contract comes into existence and awaits the owner's approval or rejection.

f: 1384. Why does the owner suffer no injustice from the Ḥanafī doctrine of bayʿ al-fuḍūlī?
b: Because the owner retains complete freedom to ratify or reject the sale.

f: 1385. What practical benefits do the Ḥanafīs identify in recognizing the sale of an unauthorized agent?
b: It spares the owner the effort of finding a buyer and negotiating, preserves the seller's legal act from being meaningless, and allows the purchaser the possibility of acquiring the property if the owner later approves.

f: 1386. What is the Ḥanafī argument for implied authority in bayʿ al-fuḍūlī?
b: There is an implied authorization by legal indication because reasonable people ordinarily consent to transactions that are beneficial to their property.

f: 1387. Until when may the owner ratify a sale concluded by an unauthorized agent (bayʿ al-fuḍūlī)?
b: The owner may ratify it only so long as the sold property still exists and the contracting parties remain as they were.

f: 1388. Why must the sold property and the contracting parties still exist for ratification of bayʿ al-fuḍūlī?
b: Because ratification operates upon the existing contract. If the contract no longer exists, there is nothing left to ratify.

f: 1389. When the owner ratifies an unauthorized sale and the price is a debt, who owns the price?
b: The debt belongs to the owner, while remaining in the unauthorized seller's possession as a trust (amānah), just as if he had been an authorized agent.

f: 1390. Why does the price belong to the owner when the owner ratifies an unauthorized sale involving a debt?
b: Because subsequent ratification is treated like prior authorization.

f: 1391. Can an unauthorized seller revoke the sale before the owner ratifies it?
b: Yes. Before ratification, the unauthorized seller may revoke the sale and free himself from its obligations.

f: 1392. Why may an unauthorized seller revoke the sale before ratification, unlike an unauthorized person contracting a marriage?
b: Because in a sale he is treated as undertaking obligations himself, whereas in marriage he merely conveys another person's declaration and acts only as an intermediary.

f: 1393. What is the ruling if the purchase price in an unauthorized sale is a specifically identified item (ʿayn muʿayyanah)?
b: Ratification is valid only if that identified item still exists.

f: 1394. When the purchase price is a specifically identified item, what does the owner's ratification validate?
b: It validates the payment, not the original contract itself.

f: 1395. After ratification of an unauthorized sale where the price was a specifically identified item, who owns that item?
b: The specifically identified item becomes the property of the unauthorized seller.

f: 1396. What must the unauthorized seller give the owner after ratification when the price was a specifically identified item?
b: He must compensate the owner with an equivalent item if it is fungible (mithlī), or its value if it is non-fungible (qīmī).

f: 1397. Why does the unauthorized seller compensate the owner when the purchase price was a specifically identified item?
b: Because, from one legal perspective, the transaction functions as though the unauthorized seller purchased the property himself, and purchases do not depend on later ratification.

f: 1398. Can the heirs ratify an unauthorized sale if the owner dies before doing so?
b: No. The heirs cannot ratify the sale.

f: 1399. Why can't the heirs ratify an unauthorized sale after the owner's death?
b: Because the sale depended upon the owner's own approval for himself, and another person's approval cannot replace it after his death.

f: 1400. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله original opinion regarding ratification when the owner does not know whether the property still exists?
b: He originally held, and Muḥammad agreed, that the ratification is valid because the original presumption is that the property continues to exist.

f: 1401. What was Abū Yūsuf's رحمه الله later opinion regarding ratification when the property's continued existence is unknown?
b: He later held that ratification is invalid until it is known that the property still exists.

f: 1402. Why did Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله later require proof that the property still exists before ratification?
b: Because the continued existence of the property is a condition of ratification, and legal rulings are not established on doubt.

f: 1403. What is the ruling if someone usurps a slave, sells him, the purchaser emancipates him, and the owner later ratifies the sale?
b: According to Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله, the emancipation becomes valid upon the owner's ratification (by istiḥsān). Muḥammad held that it is invalid.

f: 1404. Why did Muḥammad hold that the purchaser's emancipation is invalid after buying a usurped slave?
b: Because emancipation requires complete ownership, and a suspended sale does not immediately confer complete ownership.

f: 1405. Which ḥadīth did Muḥammad cite to support his view that the emancipation is invalid?
b: "There is no emancipation regarding what the son of Ādam does not own."

f: 1406. What examples did Muḥammad use to argue that incomplete ownership cannot validate emancipation?
b: (1) A usurper cannot emancipate the slave and later validate it by paying compensation. (2) A purchaser cannot emancipate property while the seller retains an option (khiyār) and later validate it by the seller's approval.

f: 1407. What additional example did Muḥammad use to show that suspended ownership cannot support legal dispositions?
b: A purchaser from a usurper cannot resell the slave before ownership is perfected.

f: 1408. According to Muḥammad, why should later compensation by the usurper not validate the purchaser's prior emancipation?
b: Because the purchaser lacked complete ownership when the emancipation was declared, and later events cannot supply the ownership that was missing.

f: 1409. Why did Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and Abū Yūsuf رحمه الله hold that the purchaser's emancipation becomes valid after the owner ratifies the sale?
